title: US officials see quiet flexibility from Moscow and Kyiv as new Ukraine talks open
summary: Washington says both sides have privately softened a little over control of eastern Ukraine, but insists territory cannot be settled before a postwar security framework.
body:
Russia and Ukraine have shown a small degree of private flexibility over who should control eastern Ukraine after the war, according to American officials speaking on the eve of the first three way peace talks since February.

Delegations from Moscow, Kyiv and Washington are meeting in the Gulf as the fifth anniversary of Russia's full scale invasion approaches. The American team includes peace envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the president's son in law, who said the aim was to address the security worries both countries will have once fighting stops and to get every party thinking seriously about the day after.

Publicly, the gap remains wide. The sharpest dispute concerns Donetsk, most of which is now under Russian occupation. Moscow wants Ukraine to hand over the parts it still holds. Kyiv wants to freeze the front line where it is, arguing that those areas are essential to its future defence.

One American official said those were stated positions and that both sides had moved slightly behind closed doors. But he added that the territorial question would not be resolved until there was clarity on what security arrangements would follow the war, and that neither issue could be finalised without the other.

For Ukraine, such arrangements would likely mean firm promises of help from allies if Russia attacks again. For Russia, they could mean its long held demand that Nato pull back from eastern Europe, an idea that alarms many European governments.

The framework under discussion includes regular security consultations, crisis hotlines and reciprocal steps to lower tensions. Officials also raised the possibility of reviving the Nato Russia Council. The talks open as Ukraine mourns a Russian strike on a village in Zaporizhzhia last week that killed at least 40 people.

title: Trump says the FBI is examining Nvidia chief's affair with an alleged Chinese spy
summary: The president said he called Jensen Huang and believes he did not know the woman worked for Beijing, as China rejected the claims and Nvidia's value fell sharply.
body:
President Donald Trump says the FBI is now looking into the relationship between Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, and a woman American intelligence officials believe was spying for China.

Mr Trump told reporters at the White House that he had phoned Mr Huang on Monday to ask how he was coping and whether he had known the woman was an intelligence agent. Mr Huang told him he had no idea, the president said, adding that he believed him and regarded him as an honourable man who was suffering a great deal. He gave no details about when the FBI inquiry began or what it covers, and the bureau would not comment.

The woman, Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was managing director of Megaspeed, a Singapore company that has done business with Nvidia. Reports say Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned senior officials in a memo last spring that the Nvidia boss was close to a suspected Chinese agent.

Beijing has dismissed the allegations as groundless and an attempt to smear China. Nvidia has ordered an independent investigation and says it has no reason to think company secrets or national security were compromised.

Mr Huang has admitted being unfaithful to his wife and apologised to his family, saying he remains committed to protecting the company and supporting American security.

Investors were less forgiving. Nvidia's shares fell about four per cent on Monday, wiping roughly 250 billion dollars off the value of a firm whose chips sit at the heart of the global race in artificial intelligence and whose exports to China Washington treats as a national security matter.

Mr Trump was pressed repeatedly on when he first learned of the relationship but would say only that he was told over a period of time. He said he expected President Xi Jinping to raise the matter when the two next meet.

title: Supreme Court clears the way for a border wall through Big Bend National Park
summary: The justices lifted a lower court order that had paused construction in the West Texas park, siding with the administration over its border security powers.
body:
The US Supreme Court has allowed the Trump administration to press ahead with a border wall through a remote stretch of Big Bend National Park in West Texas.

On Monday the court granted the government's emergency request to lift an injunction that had frozen construction while a legal challenge was heard. The justices said the order stood in the way of the government's compelling interest in securing the border, and that the administration was very likely to win its argument that the lower court had no jurisdiction.

That argument rests on a 1996 immigration law that sharply limits the power of district courts over border barriers, allowing them to hear only claims that the Constitution itself has been breached. The court found the challengers' case did not meet that test. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only member of the court to signal disagreement.

The ruling overturns, for now, an October decision by District Judge Kathleen Cardone. She had noted that the Big Bend sector covers more than a quarter of the border with Mexico but accounts for only a tiny share of migrant arrests, somewhere between 0.3 and 2.2 per cent. If that counted as an area of high illegal entry, she reasoned, then the whole frontier would.

The park's mountains and desert are home to endangered wildlife, including the Mexican long nosed bat, and opponents say a wall would scar a landscape of deep ecological and cultural value. The plan has drawn objections from conservation groups, local officials, Indigenous campaigners and some Republicans.

The administration describes the area as a corridor for irregular crossings and drug smuggling and calls the project an urgent security priority. The border wall has been a signature promise for President Trump since his first campaign for the White House.

title: Trump declares the Iran war effectively over but keeps the blockade in place
summary: After White House talks with Qatar's prime minister, the president said military action no longer looks necessary, while Tehran brushed his remarks aside as invented.
body:
President Donald Trump has signalled that he regards the war with Iran as all but finished, telling reporters at an unscheduled White House briefing on Monday that Iran was militarily spent and that America would simply hold its current position.

The remarks came after a private meeting attended by Vice President JD Vance and Qatar's prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani. The Qatari leader said afterwards that the two sides had discussed the wider region and how to move talks between Washington and Tehran forward, and he described the conversation as positive.

Holding the line, as Mr Trump framed it, does not mean easing pressure. He made clear that the naval blockade of Iranian ports would continue, alongside the newly created Task Force Iron Gate, which aims to choke off Iran's trade over land and across the Caspian Sea. He said Gulf neighbours including Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and Kuwait preferred that arrangement to renewed fighting.

He also left the door open to fresh strikes. Further military action did not seem needed for now, he said, but American forces remained ready should anything change, and he predicted the conflict would wind down fairly soon.

Tehran was unimpressed. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, accused Washington on social media of spreading false stories about talks that were not happening and urged it to give up.

Separately, President Masoud Pezeshkian said the Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, wanted an end to what he called a state of neither war nor peace. Mr Pezeshkian said Iran remained willing to negotiate but would not accept terms forced upon it.

The exchange leaves the region in an uneasy limbo: no active bombing campaign, but no settlement either, with the blockade still squeezing Iran's economy and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz still constrained.

title: Saudi Arabia's vital East West oil pipeline hit again near Medina
summary: A small fire broke out after the attack but was put out, officials said, with no casualties and no disruption to the line that lets Riyadh bypass Hormuz.
body:
Saudi Arabia says its East West oil pipeline, the kingdom's main route for exporting crude without passing through the Strait of Hormuz, came under attack again on Monday.

An official at the Ministry of Energy told the state news agency that the line was struck in the Medina region in the west of the country. The attack caused a limited fire, which crews extinguished. Nobody was hurt, the official said, and the flow of oil through the pipeline carried on as normal.

The statement did not say who was responsible. The attack comes as fighting intensifies between the Saudi backed Yemeni government coalition and the Houthi movement, which is aligned with Iran and has repeatedly fired drones and missiles at Saudi refineries, storage sites and other energy facilities.

The pipeline stretches roughly 1,200 kilometres across the desert of the Arabian Peninsula to the Red Sea coast. Its importance has soared since the war on Iran tightened traffic through Hormuz and set off a global energy crunch. Riyadh has diverted around four million barrels of crude a day along the route to the port of Yanbu, a volume equal to about four per cent of world supply.

That makes it an obvious target. The line was closed for several days in September after a wave of drone strikes that Saudi officials said had been launched from Iraq, and satellite pictures later showed repair work and new bypass sections being built near the damaged stretch.

Monday's incident appears to have been contained quickly, but each fresh strike underlines how exposed the kingdom's workaround for Hormuz has become while the regional conflict drags on.

title: Trial of man accused of killing Charlie Kirk set for June 2028
summary: A Utah judge fixed jury selection for the summer of 2028, a timetable the activist's family says is slow but one they will accept.
body:
The man accused of murdering the conservative activist Charlie Kirk will go on trial in June 2028, a judge in Utah has ruled.

Tyler Robinson, 23, denies aggravated murder and six further charges over the shooting in September 2025, when Mr Kirk, then 31, was killed while addressing an audience on a college campus in the state. Judge Tony Graf Jr told the Utah County court on Monday that jury selection would start on 21 June 2028.

The two sides had been far apart on timing. Prosecutors said they could be ready by October 2027 and were prepared to push that to January 2028 to avoid the holidays. The defence asked for more time and suggested a start in 2029. Estimates of the trial's length also differ, from 17 weeks according to the prosecution to as long as seven months according to the defence.

Mr Robinson could face the death penalty if convicted of aggravated murder, and his lawyers are trying to take that option off the table. They have also sought to keep cameras out of the courtroom.

Mr Kirk's widow, Erika, who has two children with him, had pressed for the earliest possible date and for the proceedings to be streamed live. She and his parents have attended several hearings. Her lawyer told the judge that a trial nearly three years after the killing did not feel speedy to the family, but that they had no choice but to accept it and should not have to wait any longer.

At a preliminary hearing in July, prosecutors set out evidence they say links Mr Robinson to the killing, including DNA on the weapon and other items, alleged admissions to people close to him and a recorded statement from his roommate and partner. The defence has questioned that evidence and the credentials of expert witnesses.

title: Washington joins up its agencies to speed defences against rogue drones
summary: Five federal departments have signed an agreement to test and quickly field systems that can detect, track and stop dangerous drones over American airspace.
body:
The Trump administration says it is moving faster to put counter drone systems into service, after several federal departments agreed a joint plan to tackle what officials describe as a rising threat to aviation and national security.

The Departments of Transportation, Defense, Homeland Security, Energy and Justice have signed a memorandum, under the direction of a White House task force, to assess anti drone technology and deploy it quickly. The Federal Aviation Administration announced the arrangement on Monday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the government was taking a coordinated approach across all its arms to protect American skies from modern threats and keep air travellers safe.

According to the aviation regulator, the agencies will work with it and with the Federal Communications Commission on systems able to spot, follow, halt or take control of dangerous or unauthorised drones. An official at the regulator said it had already approved more than a thousand coordination requests from the Pentagon and Homeland Security on counter drone deployments, and could clear familiar systems within a day.

Attorney General Todd Blanche recalled that five men were arrested this summer over an alleged plan to use explosive laden drones at a crowded White House event, and said his department would pursue those who endanger the public.

The move follows a decision last month to ban unauthorised drone flights up to 400 feet along the entire border with Mexico, reaching about one nautical mile inland. It also comes days after NATO stressed the need for affordable anti drone defences, with the alliance committed to spending more than $40bn on such capabilities over five years.

title: White House briefly locked down after car crash and barrier jump at Lafayette Park
summary: Two people were detained on Monday morning as the Secret Service dealt with a smoking car on the pavement and a separate intruder, with the president inside the residence.
body:
The White House was briefly sealed off on Monday after two separate security incidents in Lafayette Park, the square directly opposite the presidential residence, the Secret Service has said.

At around 10am local time, or 15:00 GMT, a driver mounted the pavement on the northern edge of the park near the junction of 16th and H Streets. Secret Service police and National Guard units rushed to the scene. Footage showed a silver saloon pouring out smoke as officers surrounded it, and the driver climbing out and lashing out at them before being arrested. The agency said the man had been combative but was quickly detained. A police bomb disposal team was then brought in to check the vehicle.

At roughly the same moment, a second person climbed over a security barrier at the park's northwest corner and was also taken into custody. Officials have not said whether the two events were linked.

President Donald Trump was inside the executive residence at the time. The building was placed under lockdown and nearby roads were closed, with restrictions lifted about an hour later, according to reporters travelling with the president.

Authorities have not disclosed what charges either person may face, and both incidents remain under investigation.

title: Republican rebel Massie moves to force a House vote on impeaching Hegseth
summary: The Kentucky congressman says the defence secretary broke the law by waging war on Iran for more than 90 days without Congress, and wants Trump to replace him now.
body:
Thomas Massie, a Republican congressman from Kentucky, has formally tabled articles of impeachment against Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and intends to force a vote in the House of Representatives this week.

Mr Massie argues that by keeping American forces in hostilities with Iran for over 90 days without authorisation from Congress, Mr Hegseth has broken the law and the Constitution. He also accuses him of intimidating critics of the administration, seizing foreign leaders and ignoring war powers resolutions passed by lawmakers.

He introduced the resolution on the House floor on Monday afternoon. Speaker Mike Johnson now has two days to bring it forward, and the chamber can vote on it directly, send it to a committee or set it aside.

Mr Massie, who lost his own seat earlier this year and has opposed the Iran war since it began nearly nine months ago, says his aim is partly to spare the administration something worse. He has called his effort a much gentler version of the hearings and trials Democrats will hold once they take over Congress in January, and urged President Donald Trump to replace Mr Hegseth while a successor can still be confirmed by the current Senate.

Mr Hegseth told reporters he was not worried and said he would hold a news conference on Tuesday on the subject, his first since May.

House Democrats are expected to back the move, and their leader Hakeem Jeffries has already said he is a firm yes. Republicans currently hold 218 seats to the Democrats' 214, and one public affairs professor in Washington said the measure could pass if enough unhappy Republicans simply stay away. Removal, however, would need a two thirds vote in the Senate, a bar that looks out of reach both now and after January.

Only two cabinet members have ever been impeached by the House, and the Senate convicted neither. The same professor suggested Mr Trump is more likely to dismiss Mr Hegseth himself than to see Congress remove him.

title: Nvidia loses about $250bn in value as board investigates Huang affair
summary: Shares in the American chip giant fell around 6% on Monday after its board ordered an inquiry into the chief executive's relationship with a woman US officials call a Chinese spy.
body:
Roughly $250bn was wiped off the market value of Nvidia on Monday after the American chipmaker said it would hold an independent investigation into its chief executive, Jensen Huang.

The shares fell by about 6% after Mr Huang admitted an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, whom American intelligence officials reportedly regard as working for Beijing. She was managing director of a Singapore company, Megaspeed, that has done business with Nvidia. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is reported to have warned senior officials in a memo last spring about the relationship.

The board said it was acting in light of reporting that Mr Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort, while stressing that it had no reason to think company secrets or national security had been compromised. Mr Huang apologised to his wife and children, said he was committed to protecting the company and American security, and pledged to cooperate. China's foreign ministry dismissed the spying claims as baseless and an attempt to smear the country.

He has also been asked to attend a closed briefing for several congressional committees next week. Three Republican committee chairmen wrote that the reports raised serious concerns about Chinese access to sensitive American technology.

President Donald Trump called Mr Huang an honourable man, and other technology leaders including Elon Musk backed him to stay on. Rival chipmakers gained as the wider market opened higher.

One market strategist argued the damage would be brief because Nvidia sits at the heart of the AI boom, though she noted there is no obvious successor. Unlike many founders, Mr Huang owns only about 3.5% of the company under a single class share structure, leaving him exposed to any board decision. The strategist said she expected the board to keep him unless clear wrongdoing emerged, but to start grooming a deputy.

Nvidia's chips are central to the technology race between Washington and Beijing, and the administration agreed in January to let it sell its H200 processors to Chinese buyers under conditions.

title: France blames Iran's Revolutionary Guards for sabotaging supermarket freezers
summary: Paris says an IRGC linked hacking unit pushed up temperatures in fridges at hundreds of French shops last month, spoiling tons of food, and promises sanctions.
body:
France has formally pointed the finger at Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps over a wave of hacking last month that sent temperatures soaring inside supermarket fridges and freezers across the country.

Foreign Minister Jean Noël Barrot described the operation as unmatched in its size and aggression and called it the first large scale act of cyber sabotage on French soil. He said the Iranian ambassador had been summoned to receive a firm protest, that those responsible would face sanctions, and that Paris would take further proportionate steps to discourage anyone from trying again.

The Paris prosecutor, Laure Beccuau, has opened an investigation targeting the head of an offensive hacking unit known as Shahid Kaveh and two of his deputies. She said the group is tied to the Guards' electronic and cyber centre, and it is widely thought to work directly for the Iranian state.

The intrusion began on 11 October, when attackers took over remote temperature control software made by a Danish engineering company and used by many French grocers. More than a hundred Coopérative U stores and around 180 Intermarché and Netto shops were affected, along with outlets of other big chains. In some stores the cabinets reportedly reached 50C overnight, and large quantities of chilled and frozen food had to be thrown away.

A second round earlier this month struck more than a hundred shops elsewhere in Europe, mainly in Belgium and Luxembourg, with smaller numbers in several Nordic and Baltic countries, Ireland and the Netherlands. It is not yet known whether the two waves are connected. Fridges at a few American military bases also failed in August in incidents now being examined as possible sabotage.

Tehran has not given an official reply, though some Iranian media have rejected the accusation as groundless. Two hacktivist groups aligned with Russia had claimed responsibility last week, but their claims were widely doubted.

France has not explained how it reached its conclusion, and attributing cyber attacks is notoriously difficult. The accusation comes as some Iranian politicians argue that any retaliation should reach beyond the Middle East if the American and Israeli war on Iran resumes.

title: Trump casts doubt on the midterm results days after saying he would accept them
summary: The president asked online whether anyone really believed last week's vote was honest, offering no evidence, as officials across the country report a largely smooth count.
body:
President Donald Trump has begun questioning whether the midterm elections that handed both chambers of Congress to the Democrats were fair, only days after saying he was fully prepared to accept the outcome.

In a post on his social media platform on Monday, he asked whether anybody truly thought the election had been honest and wondered how the polls could have been so far off. He referred loosely to vote dumps and machines but gave no detail of what he meant or any evidence of error or wrongdoing.

On election night he had said he was absolutely willing to accept the results and expected to work something out with the Democrats. Since then he has also argued that his party would have won comfortably had he been on the ballot, and has conceded in a television interview that higher petrol prices caused by the Iran war hurt Republicans. Vice President JD Vance has made a similar case.

Democrats currently hold 54 Senate seats and 254 House seats, comfortable majorities in both chambers, while contests including the Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi are still being counted. State and local officials say voting went largely without trouble, apart from some closures caused by extreme weather and a handful of administrative or technical delays.

An election scholar at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology said results were reported in the usual patterns seen across the country, with some states such as Florida and Georgia posting early numbers quickly because early and postal ballots had already been tallied. A Harvard election law specialist said slower counts in some states reflect local law and practicalities, not anything sinister.

Polling before the vote had pointed to Republican losses in both chambers. Mr Trump spent months alleging that the 2020 presidential election was rigged, claims repeatedly rejected by the courts, and his Justice Department filed lawsuits shortly before these midterms challenging counts in states including California and Alaska. Judges ruled against it in almost every case.

title: Can a small American unit really seal Iran off? Analysts are sceptical
summary: Trump says almost nothing now moves in or out of Iran, but experts doubt the new Iron Gate task force can police its land borders and warn it may widen the war.
body:
President Donald Trump has declared that Iran is now all but cut off from the outside world, pointing to a fresh American effort aimed at its overland supply routes. Specialists in defence and the region are far from convinced.

The claim followed an announcement by US Central Command of Task Force Iron Gate, a unit meant to stop Tehran moving advanced weapons, components with both civilian and military uses, sanctioned goods and illicit money across its land frontiers and the Caspian Sea. Working from Tampa in Florida alongside other government agencies, it is designed to complement the naval blockade around the Strait of Hormuz. The president wrote on Sunday that the task force was fully in effect.

Analysts describe it as essentially an intelligence hub that would draw on satellites, drones, intercepted communications and financial tracking, and could feed pressure on foreign suppliers. One British defence scholar noted that a team of around twenty people cannot watch thousands of kilometres of border, and said the real aim is probably to make Iranian procurement slower, costlier and riskier rather than to halt it outright. Some expect the intelligence to lead to strikes or covert raids to seize shipments.

The larger obstacle is political. Iraq offers some leverage, yet networks loyal to Tehran run deep there. Azerbaijan might help quietly, Turkmenistan is wary of upsetting Russia and China, Pakistan is busy mediating between the two sides and Turkey has little appetite for a new border dispute. Without American access to the Caspian, one regional academic said, the effort may be largely symbolic. Reports that Russian drone parts reach Iran across that sea make the task tougher still.

Critics also warn of mission creep. Intelligence gathering could slide into seizures, border closures or strikes on neighbouring soil, and Iran could answer by squeezing shipping in Hormuz or leaning on the Houthis near Bab al Mandeb. A former senior counterterrorism official argued the move invites escalation just as the vice president tries to negotiate with Tehran.

title: Tanker ablaze near Hormuz after Revolutionary Guards say they hit three ships
summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say they attacked three tankers on Sunday for using routes it had not approved in coordination with the US military.
body:
An oil tanker was seen burning close to the Strait of Hormuz after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it had attacked three tankers on Sunday.

The Guards accused the vessels of taking what they called unauthorised routes through the waterway while working with the American military, which has been coordinating a shuttle system to keep some oil moving through the strait during the war.

Tehran has repeatedly warned ships that leaving the corridors it designates could expose them to attack. Iranian state television said on Monday that 11 tankers had been targeted over the previous ten days, and that four of them were unable to carry on with their voyages. Media close to the Guards also claimed that navigation systems in the southern part of the strait were hit overnight, halting tankers that were due to pass under the American arrangement.

The latest incidents add to the strain on one of the world's most important energy routes, through which a large share of the Gulf's oil and gas exports normally travels, and come as mediators try to stop the conflict between Washington and Tehran from returning to full scale fighting.

title: Los Angeles elects a democratic socialist mayor as the movement gains ground
summary: Nithya Raman unseated Karen Bass with almost 53 per cent of the vote, the latest sign that left wing candidates are winning big American races.
body:
Los Angeles is set to be run by a democratic socialist after city council member Nithya Raman defeated the sitting mayor, Karen Bass, taking close to 53 per cent of the vote. The result was declared on 5 November.

Raman, 45, a former urban planner who campaigned on making the city simply function better on housing and homelessness, thanked voters in a video and said change would be hard and would take time. She takes office in December.

Her victory puts the second largest city in the United States alongside New York, Seattle, Providence and Washington DC, all of which have or will soon have mayors from the same political tradition. Observers link the trend to a widespread sense that the economy is stacked in favour of the rich, and to the struggle many Americans face in paying for basic needs.

The midterm elections offered further evidence. The Democratic Socialists of America say they have quadrupled their numbers in Congress. Three candidates backed by New York mayor Zohran Mamdani, Brad Lander, Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier, won seats for the first time. In Colorado, Melat Kiros, a 29 year old who came to the country from Ethiopia, won after beating a sitting Democrat in the primary, and in Los Angeles Angela Gonzales Torres ousted congressman Jimmy Gomez.

The group says enthusiasm and door knocking help it overcome the funding edge of establishment rivals. An October poll found half of voters would consider backing a democratic socialist, a striking change from a decade ago when Bernie Sanders was widely dismissed.

Success has brought internal strains. Days before the vote, a national panel of the organisation narrowly rejected, by 14 votes to 13, a move to withdraw its endorsement of Raman over her past positions on Israel. Supporters say the focus now is on delivering everyday services, an approach that echoes the practical municipal socialism of the early twentieth century.

title: Tehran refuses to budge on its terms despite fresh strikes on Qeshm
summary: Iran insists its seven point plan is still the most sensible route to peace, as American pressure grows and mediators race to head off a wider war.
body:
Iran says new American strikes will not change the conditions it has set for ending the war, even as Washington keeps up military pressure and dismisses parts of its plan.

A deputy governor of Hormozgan province confirmed on Monday that the island of Qeshm had been hit overnight, adding that homes, businesses and vital infrastructure were not damaged. The United States did not directly confirm the raid, but Secretary of State Marco Rubio again described recent attacks on the island as defensive. Earlier strikes have targeted Iranian air defences and radar sites.

Tehran's list of seven demands includes lifting the American blockade of its southern ports and removing sanctions, and largely amounts to a return to a memorandum agreed with Washington in Islamabad in June, with new conditions on the future of Hormuz. Rubio has called some of them unrealistic. Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei rejected that view, arguing the plan could restore security to the strait and open the way to a wider process. He also dismissed a new American reward of up to $20m for information on the nuclear programme as an attempt to keep the issue alive after heavy Republican losses in the midterms.

Iran says it will not hand over its highly enriched uranium, thought to lie beneath the ruins of bombed sites, though it is willing to dilute it. Inspectors currently have access only to the Bushehr power plant.

Hopes rest partly on a White House meeting between President Donald Trump and Qatar's prime minister. A London based defence analyst said Washington's main objection is that Tehran wants the benefits of a deal before making concessions, and that neither the US nor Iran's Arab neighbours would accept Iranian controlled shipping lanes in the long term.

At sea, the Revolutionary Guards deny American claims that all mines have been cleared, and state television says 11 tankers have been attacked in ten days. Trump has played down a return to all out war but said 38 bridges are among targets if fighting resumes on a large scale.

title: Little hope of a breakthrough as Russia, Ukraine and America meet again
summary: Analysts expect no peace deal from this week's three way talks, with territory and security guarantees still dividing Moscow and Kyiv.
body:
Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the United States gather on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi for a fourth round of peace talks this year, but few who follow the war expect much to come of it.

Washington's team will be led by envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, in the first such meeting for nine months. Ukraine sends its intelligence chief Rustem Umerov at the head of a group that includes presidential chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov. Moscow's delegation is led by former culture minister Vladimir Medinsky. The Kremlin said on Monday no European officials would take part, contradicting France, which had said officials from Paris, London, Berlin, NATO and the European Commission would attend. An EU official later said security advisers from those capitals would be on site, without clarifying their role.

The mood has been shaped by President Donald Trump's recent dealings with Moscow. He has blamed President Volodymyr Zelensky for stalling, urged Kyiv to give up land and approved a deal to buy Russian diesel. Russia holds about a fifth of Ukraine, including Crimea.

Analysts say the core gaps are unchanged. Kyiv wants Russian troops out and firm guarantees for its security; Moscow refuses to withdraw, rejects NATO membership for Ukraine and opposes foreign troops on its soil afterwards. A Ukrainian MP said he expected no real progress because the Kremlin is not serious, while a former American diplomat said Vladimir Putin's method is to demand everything, escalate and wait for others to give way. Experts also warn that a deal forced on Ukraine could leave Moldova, Georgia and other former Soviet states exposed.

Some smaller gains are possible, a Kyiv professor suggested, such as arrangements on grain, a pause in fighting at sea or on energy targets, and another prisoner swap. One economist added that Trump, weakened by the midterms, may focus more on foreign policy and press Kyiv harder for concessions.

title: American talk of a new European security order worries allies before Ukraine talks
summary: European officials fear Washington's call for a broader security framework for the continent hands Moscow an early gain.
body:
Even before Russian and Ukrainian negotiators sit down with American mediators this week, European officials and analysts fear that Washington has already given Moscow something it wanted.

Their concern centres on a call by American negotiators for a broader security architecture for Europe. To many in European capitals, that language closely mirrors arguments the Kremlin has made for years, when it has complained that NATO's growth to the east threatens Russia and has pressed for a redrawn order on the continent.

Critics worry that framing the talks this way widens the agenda beyond ending the fighting in Ukraine and could put the continent's existing alliances up for discussion, while Kyiv and its partners still lack firm guarantees of their own. Europe is not formally a party to the three way talks, and the Kremlin has insisted no European officials will be at the table.

The unease adds to doubts about how much the new round can achieve, with territory and future protection for Ukraine still the hardest questions to resolve.

title: Thirteen dead as boat carrying Sudanese migrants sinks off Crete
summary: Greek rescuers saved 18 people, all from Sudan, after a boat that had spent days at sea in strong winds went down south of the island.
body:
At least 13 people have died after a migrant boat sank off the Greek island of Crete, with all 18 survivors identified as Sudanese.

The Greek coastguard said four of those rescued, among them a toddler, were taken to hospital. Officials said the cause of death was not yet clear, but they believe the vessel had been adrift for several days and had been unable to make land because of strong winds. A container ship sailing under the Moroccan flag spotted the boat about 15 nautical miles from the coast, and a coastguard official described the survivors as shaking with cold.

The coastguard picked up another 187 people in three separate operations around Greece on the same day.

Crete has become one of the main entry points for people trying to reach Europe from North Africa and the Middle East. More than 22,000 of the roughly 86,400 people who have arrived by sea this year landed there, and around 1,700 reached the island in the first three days of November alone. United Nations figures show more than 37,000 arrivals in Greece so far in 2026, already above the total for the whole of last year. Athens has announced plans including a temporary housing complex near Heraklion.

Crossings from Libya have risen sharply in recent years, driven in large part by people escaping the war in Sudan, which has displaced millions and pushed many to attempt the dangerous journey across the Mediterranean.

title: Nine foreigners held in South Africa on suspicion of heading to fight in Ukraine war
summary: Police say the young men were stopped as they prepared to fly out, but have not said which side they intended to join.
body:
South African police have arrested nine foreign nationals they say were trying to leave the country to take part in the war between Russia and Ukraine.

The group, aged between 20 and 26, were detained on Sunday evening at OR Tambo, the country's busiest airport, and at a hotel in Bruma, east of Johannesburg, in an operation that involved Interpol. Officers said they were getting ready to board flights, though their final destination has not been made public.

Authorities have not revealed the nationalities of the suspects beyond saying none of them lived in South Africa, and have not said whether they planned to fight for Moscow or Kyiv or who arranged their travel. They are accused of breaking South African law, which bans mercenary activity without government approval, and police said the involvement of international agencies suggested laws in their home countries had also been broken. They are due in court on Monday or Tuesday.

The case highlights the growing pull of the conflict on Africa. A Ukrainian intelligence estimate earlier this year put the number of Africans recruited by Russia at more than 1,700, from 36 countries, some of whom say they were misled about where they were going. Kenya has said 252 of its citizens were illegally drafted and reached an agreement with Moscow in March to stop recruitment. Ghana reported in February that 55 of its nationals had been killed. South Africa brought home 17 citizens that month who were allegedly tricked into joining, and last December arrested five people, including a journalist, accused of recruiting fighters. Ukraine has also enlisted foreign volunteers, including Africans.

title: Deportees passed on to countries the US itself may not send them to
summary: Partner governments that take in people deported by Washington are moving them onward to nations that American courts have barred as destinations.
body:
People removed from the United States are being sent back to the very countries that American judges ordered they must not be returned to, through an arrangement that relies on foreign governments acting as a staging post.

Under the system, partner states agree to receive deportees from the Trump administration. Those governments then move the new arrivals on to other nations, including places where the United States would be legally forbidden from sending them directly because of the risk they face there.

The practice raises sharp questions about the principle in international law that bars returning anyone to a country where they could be persecuted or harmed. Court orders protecting individual migrants are meant to prevent exactly that outcome, yet the onward transfers appear to achieve it at one remove.

The finding lands at a sensitive moment for the White House, which is weighing how hard to press its deportation drive after heavy losses in last week's midterm elections and with a new chief of staff closely tied to the policy. With Democrats about to gain more power in Congress, the arrangements could face closer scrutiny in the months ahead.

title: Candidates who ran on health care sweep into office across America
summary: Doctors and public health figures did well in the midterms, as voters worried about measles and food safety rewarded health focused campaigns.
body:
A wave of candidates who put health at the heart of their campaigns won office in last week's midterm elections, a result that could reshape policy at national, state and local level.

Among the winners were Annie Andrews and Abdul El Sayed, both of whom built their pitch to voters around public health. Their success is being read by supporters as a sign of hope at a time when, in their view, the Trump administration has been dismantling much of the country's health policy.

Voters went to the polls against a backdrop of a rare rise in diseases that vaccines can prevent, measles chief among them, as well as serious outbreaks of illness linked to contaminated food. Many chose candidates who promised to put public health first, bring down the cost of care and protect reproductive health.

Some of those elected have also backed the impeachment of Robert F Kennedy Jr, the health secretary, whose handling of vaccines has been a lightning rod for criticism. With Democrats set to hold more power in Congress, the new arrivals could press for changes to national health policy in the coming session.

title: Trump to host Qatar's prime minister as push to end the Iran war gathers pace
summary: The White House meeting comes as efforts to stop the conflict intensify after the midterms, though officials on both sides warn a deal is not close.
body:
Donald Trump is due to meet the prime minister of Qatar on Monday, as diplomacy aimed at ending the war with Iran picks up speed in the wake of last week's midterm elections.

Qatar has been one of the main go betweens in the conflict, and its leaders have kept channels open with Tehran throughout more than eight months of fighting. The talks at the White House are expected to focus on whether any path exists towards a lasting settlement.

Senior American and Gulf officials have nonetheless played down hopes of an imminent breakthrough. With no clear victory in sight, the president has suggested that a return to major combat is unlikely in the near future, but he has so far refused to accept a truce plan already put forward by Iran.

The meeting also comes as Trump grapples with the political fallout at home, having conceded over the weekend that parts of his immigration policy may have been too harsh. Allies in the region will be watching closely for any sign that the White House is ready to shift its position on the war.

title: Washington orders Lebanon's consul general in Detroit to leave
summary: The secretary of state acted after old social media posts resurfaced that appeared to praise the 1983 bombing of the Marine barracks in Beirut.
body:
The United States has ordered Lebanon's consul general in Detroit to leave the country, after social media posts attributed to him resurfaced and drew outrage in Washington.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Ibrahim Charara to depart over posts that allegedly praised the 1983 attack on the Marine barracks in Beirut. The 1983 bombing, which Washington blames on Hezbollah, killed 241 American service members.

The expulsion of a serving diplomat is a rare step and is likely to add strain to relations between Washington and Beirut at a delicate time for Lebanon, where the armed group remains a powerful force.

Detroit and the surrounding area are home to one of the largest Lebanese communities in America, making the consulate an important link for families on both sides of the Atlantic.

title: Drones set major Russian refinery alight as Odesa counts its dead
summary: At least four people were killed in a night of strikes, with Ukraine hitting the Kirishi plant near St Petersburg and Russia pounding Odesa and the power grid.
body:
Russia and Ukraine exchanged heavy blows overnight, leaving at least four people dead and one of Russia's biggest oil refineries on fire.

In the Black Sea port of Odesa, a Russian attack killed three people, according to the head of the city's military administration. A fourth person was badly hurt.

Far to the north, Ukrainian drones struck the Kirishi refinery in the Leningrad region, the second largest in Russia. The regional governor said a woman was killed by falling debris and a flat in the town was damaged. He claimed air defences brought down 113 drones over the region during the night. The area is a key route for Russian oil and grain shipped out through the Baltic.

Ukraine's military chief of staff said forces also hit the Morozov plant near St Petersburg, which makes explosives and fuel used in missiles fired at Ukrainian cities. Russian state media reported that Moscow's forces struck three power substations and a cargo ship in the Black Sea it said was carrying weapons for Kyiv.

Ukraine's energy ministry counted 128 Russian attacks on the energy system over the past week, part of what it describes as a campaign to wreck heating and power supplies before winter. President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv, Dnipro, Sumy, Donetsk and Kherson regions were worst affected, and announced an emergency arrangement agreed with the European Commission so that European money can reach damaged infrastructure faster.

The strikes come days before a fresh round of negotiations in the Gulf between Russia and Ukraine, with the United States in the chair. The Kremlin insisted the talks will remain a three way affair, after France said European representatives would take part. Zelensky said he had aligned his position with Brussels beforehand, while unease persists in Europe over the president's talk of a very big deal with Moscow covering the whole continent.

title: Support for Israel in Washington frays in both parties
summary: Republicans including the vice president are calling for change, while many Democrats push to restrict military aid, ending a long era of near automatic backing.
body:
The broad agreement across American politics on support for Israel is weakening, with voices in both major parties now pressing for new limits on the relationship.

On the Republican side, Vice President JD Vance is among those who have called for a change of course. Among Democrats, a large number of lawmakers have been leading a campaign to place restrictions on the military aid that Washington sends to Israel.

For decades, backing for Israel was one of the few issues on which leaders of both parties reliably agreed. That consensus now looks far less secure than at any point in recent memory.

The results of last week's midterm elections, which handed Democrats more power in Congress, are likely to sharpen the debate. Any attempt to attach conditions to aid would mark a significant break with past practice and could become a defining fight of the new session.

title: Sudanese children who fled war struggle to survive on the streets of Cairo
summary: Three years of conflict have pushed hundreds of thousands of young Sudanese out of school, and many who reached Egypt now face gangs, drugs and deep trauma.
body:
Children who escaped the civil war in Sudan are reaching a breaking point in a neglected corner of Cairo, where rubbish piles up, sewage runs in the open and drug dealers and gangs move through the streets after dark.

Three years of fighting at home have left hundreds of thousands of Sudanese children without schooling, and those who made it to Egypt are often exposed to new dangers as soon as they arrive. Many carry deep wounds from what they saw before they fled.

A social worker who supports these families describes her work as an effort to pull badly traumatised young refugees back from the edge. One case she recounts is that of an eight year old boy who repeatedly told his mother he wanted to die so that he could be with his father, who was killed in Sudan before the family left.

Egypt has become a refuge for many families displaced by the war, yet for children like these, safety across the border has not meant an end to danger or grief.

title: Iran tightens its grip at home as threat of new US strikes looms
summary: Authorities are warning of harsh sentences for protesters and reimposing controls in public spaces after months of looser rules during the war.
body:
Iran's security services are on high alert and taking a harder line with anything they see as a threat to the state's control, as the country braces for the possibility of a fresh and wider wave of American attacks.

Officials have warned the public that anyone who protests against the government can expect severe punishment. They are also reasserting control over public spaces, including rules on how people dress, after months in which enforcement had eased. Areas of Tehran that have become popular gathering spots for young people are among those now drawing attention from the authorities.

Analysts say the message is that the Islamic Republic will not bend on its founding principles after eight months of war. A Gulf studies expert at Qatar University said the state has also managed to rally supporters in public, not only from the Revolutionary Guards but from among civilians, and expects this to continue until the fighting ends.

On Sunday the judiciary announced the execution of three young men detained during the nationwide protests in January, accusing them of attacking government buildings near Tehran on behalf of the United States and Israel. Tehran calls those protests an attempted coup. A United Nations fact finding mission, however, concluded that the crackdown on demonstrators amounted to crimes against humanity, and rights groups say thousands were killed, most of them on two nights in early January.

A rights group based in Norway says Iran has executed at least 79 political or religious prisoners this year, among them 40 people arrested during the January unrest, some after spying convictions. Groups abroad say many such cases are tainted by claims of torture and forced confessions.

One political scientist argued that the leadership is behaving much as any government would when facing powerful enemies, noting that rules on headscarves, alcohol and other social matters have at times been relaxed. Repression, he said, has been kept mainly for political dissent and challenges to the system itself.

title: Stephen Miller takes over as White House chief of staff
summary: The architect of Trump's immigration crackdown begins his first day in the most powerful staff job in the White House, just as the president concedes deportations went too far.
body:
Stephen Miller starts work on Monday as White House chief of staff, a promotion that hands the president's most divisive adviser even greater sway over the administration.

Miller, 41, has been at Donald Trump's side since the start of his political career, first as a speechwriter on the 2016 campaign. He became known as the driving force behind some of the most contested policies of the first Trump term, including the separation of families at the southern border and the ban on travellers from a number of Muslim majority countries, and he has shaped the sweeping deportation drive of the second.

In his first public comments after the appointment was announced, Miller promised total loyalty and unwavering commitment to the president. Critics fear the move signals that the White House will press ahead with its hardline immigration agenda rather than soften it.

The timing is awkward. Over the weekend Trump told a television interviewer that his deportation policy had been too tough, that it had hurt him politically in the midterm elections and that he was open to a deal with Democrats that could let some undocumented immigrants stay. How that sits with the elevation of the man most closely linked to the crackdown will be one of the first tests of the new arrangement in the West Wing.

title: At least 25 seafarers dead as Iran war turns Hormuz into a deadly passage
summary: Merchant crews from far beyond the region are paying a heavy price as attacks on shipping around the Strait of Hormuz continue nine months into the war.
body:
Civilian sailors have become some of the quieter casualties of the war on Iran. The International Maritime Organization has counted at least 25 seafarers killed since the fighting began on 28 February, and at least 129 incidents involving commercial ships in and around the Strait of Hormuz.

The waterway once carried roughly a fifth of the oil the world consumes. After the United States and Israel opened their campaign, Iran effectively shut the strait and warned that ships moving without its permission could be hit, while Washington placed a naval blockade on Iranian ports. Vessels have since been struck by missiles, projectiles and sea mines, leaving some ablaze and others on the seabed.

The pace has not slowed. October was the worst month so far, with at least 31 ships hit. Last Thursday Iranian forces reported fires aboard five tankers and a tug in separate incidents, and on Sunday the Revolutionary Guard said three tankers it accused of using an unauthorised route had suffered blasts and serious fires. A tanker flagged in the Marshall Islands also exploded north of Qatar, killing one crew member.

Indian nationals have suffered most, with at least 16 dead. Three were killed in June in American strikes on merchant ships near Oman, which led New Delhi to summon a senior US diplomat, and a sailor from Gujarat died last week when his cargo vessel was hit off the Omani coast, although 13 shipmates were rescued. Two Filipino crew members died in September aboard a Saudi tanker, and an Iranian maritime union said in May that at least 44 Iranian seafarers had been killed.

Shipping industry representatives say crews going about their work have been put in harm's way through no fault of their own, and that the strain on mental health is growing. The maritime body said in late summer that about 6,000 sailors were stuck near the strait, raising wider questions about whether crews can refuse dangerous voyages and what protection international law really offers them.

title: On the Berlin Wall anniversary, Palestinians point to the barrier still rising in the West Bank
summary: The barrier through the occupied West Bank is far longer and taller than the one that split Berlin, and it sits inside a dense web of checkpoints and permits.
body:
Thirty seven years after the Berlin Wall came down on 9 November 1989, Palestinians are using the date, as they have since 2003, to draw attention to the barrier that still divides the occupied West Bank.

Israel began building it in 2002. Its planned route of 712km would make it more than four times the length of the 155km wall that ringed West Berlin for 28 years, and in towns its concrete panels stand about nine metres high, more than double the height of Berlin's. In 2004 the International Court of Justice found the barrier illegal. United Nations figures show that by April about 456km, close to two thirds of the plan, had been completed, and that around 85 per cent of the route lies inside the West Bank rather than along the 1949 armistice line.

That route decides who is cut off from what. More than 14,000 Palestinians live in the strip between the barrier and the armistice line and must cross checkpoints to reach shops, services and relatives. Roughly 150 communities own farmland in that area and can only reach it with permits and through about 62 agricultural gates, most of which stay shut for much of the year. During the 2025 olive harvest nearly three quarters of those gates opened on only a limited number of days. In Qalqiliya the barrier wraps around much of the city, turning short trips into long detours.

The wall is only one piece of a wider system. By December the UN had logged 925 checkpoints, road gates, earth mounds and other obstacles across the West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem, affecting the movement of about 3.4 million people. For activists, the Berlin comparison carries a hopeful message: barriers that once seemed permanent can still fall.

title: Rubio admits the Iran war is unpopular but insists it had to be fought
summary: The US secretary of state defended the conflict as a way to stop Tehran getting a nuclear weapon and dismissed Iran's terms for peace as unrealistic.
body:
Marco Rubio has conceded that the American war with Iran does not enjoy wide public support, while arguing that it was the right call to keep Tehran from building a nuclear bomb.

Speaking to reporters in Florida on Sunday, the secretary of state said President Donald Trump had spotted a genuine danger in Iran and acted to stop it. Taking on hard security problems, he suggested, was rarely a popular business but sometimes an essential one.

Rubio offered little hope of an early end to the fighting through talks. He said the two sides were not close to a breakthrough and, although the president would rather settle matters through diplomacy, he described the demands coming from Tehran as unacceptable and, in places, absurd and detached from reality.

His remarks followed comments by Mr Trump about Vice President JD Vance, who last week linked the war to the heavy Republican losses in the midterm elections. The president said many people had disliked what Mr Vance said, and that while he largely agreed with his deputy, he had no regrets about going to war. He predicted the campaign would be remembered as one of his administration's finest decisions and warned that a nuclear armed Iran would be a threat to the whole world.

In a separate telephone interview on Sunday, Mr Trump said renewed American strikes would probably not be needed as long as negotiations kept moving and Tehran signed a robust agreement.

Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, struck a defiant note in an online message, saying American voters had spoken and it was now for the White House to decide. He said Tehran's offer to act within two days still stood if its conditions were met, including an end to fighting on every front, but warned of a fierce response if Washington chose war. Iran has said it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz to merchant shipping within that window.

Mr Trump is due to receive the Qatari prime minister and foreign minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, at the White House on Monday, while Tehran studies proposals from Doha aimed at narrowing the gap with Washington. Rubio has also brushed aside recent talk that he might step down to seek higher office.

title: Trump concedes his deportation drive went too far and offers Democrats a deal
summary: In a rare admission after the midterm rout, the president said his immigration crackdown may have been too harsh and cost him votes.
body:
Donald Trump has acknowledged that his sweeping deportation campaign may have been too severe, and has signalled that he is willing to reach an immigration agreement with Democrats after his party's heavy defeat in last week's midterm elections.

In a television interview broadcast on Sunday, the president was asked whether the crackdown had gone too far. He replied that it probably had been too tough, adding that while many Americans welcomed it, many others felt it was excessive. He said the policy had both helped and hurt him politically.

Mr Trump also said he was open to an arrangement that would let some undocumented immigrants remain in the United States, a notable shift for a leader who made mass removals a central promise of his return to the White House.

The admission is unusual. Large scale raids by federal immigration agents have defined his second term, and the issue has been among the most divisive in American politics. Democrats, who are set to control both chambers of Congress from January, campaigned heavily on the human cost of the raids.

Yet the tone of the interview sits awkwardly with the president's decision on Friday to promote Stephen Miller, the chief architect of the immigration crackdown, to White House chief of staff. Industries that depend on immigrant labour had already voiced alarm at that appointment, and the White House said only a day earlier that it would not slow the pace of enforcement.

Elsewhere, Mr Trump has claimed the elections were a setback for the country and indicated he will resist many demands from the new Democratic majority, leaving it unclear how far any compromise on immigration might go.

Any deal would need to pass a Congress that Democrats will soon lead, and party leaders have so far put healthcare, tariffs and oversight of the administration at the top of their agenda.

title: Biden says cancer will curb promotion of his new memoir
summary: The former president said his aggressive prostate cancer is slowing him down and he will do fewer events for the book than he had hoped.
body:
Former President Joe Biden has said his health will limit how much he can do to promote his forthcoming memoir.

Mr Biden, who is being treated for an aggressive form of prostate cancer, said the illness was slowing him down and that he would not be able to take part in as many conversations and appearances around the book as he had originally planned.

The former president, who left office in January 2025, disclosed his diagnosis last year.

The remarks offer a rare personal update from Mr Biden, who has largely kept out of public view, and come days after midterm elections in which his Democratic Party won control of both chambers of Congress.

title: Rubio says security guarantees for Ukraine will top the agenda at new peace talks
summary: Washington reports progress on what protection Ukraine and Europe could have after the war, as Trump predicts a settlement that changes Ukraine's borders.
body:
The United States says it has made some headway in defining how Ukraine and the wider European continent might be protected once the war with Russia ends, ahead of a fresh round of negotiations this week.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on Sunday, before leaving for Paris to meet foreign ministers from the G7 group of wealthy democracies, that the question of security guarantees had come up again and again throughout American contacts with Moscow and Kyiv. He said progress had been made on what that security framework could look like and suggested the coming talks might move things further.

Russian and Ukrainian delegations are due to meet under American mediation on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi. Washington will be represented by its envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the president's son in law.

President Donald Trump, in a television interview aired on Sunday, said he expected the war to end soon and hinted that Ukraine could come out of any settlement with different borders, saying the country would end up a slightly different shape. Asked whether his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, was playing for time, he said he did not believe so.

The comments are likely to unsettle Kyiv, which has long resisted any deal that would formalise Russian control of occupied land. Ukrainian officials have also accused Moscow of stepping up missile and drone attacks on power stations and other infrastructure in the run up to the talks, in an effort to put pressure on their negotiators. Recent strikes have left hundreds of thousands of people without electricity as winter approaches.

European governments have been preparing for a possible role in policing a ceasefire, and many are watching closely for any sign that Washington might agree terms with Moscow over their heads. The G7 meeting in Paris is expected to give allies a chance to press Rubio on the details.

title: Trump says Dana White press secretary offer was only a joke
summary: A day after publicly urging the UFC chief to take the briefing room podium, the president told reporters he had never been serious.
body:
Donald Trump has walked back his surprise offer to make Dana White, the head of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, the next White House press secretary, saying on Sunday that he had only been joking.

Talking to reporters as he returned to Washington from his Florida beach club, the president said he had simply enjoyed imagining his friend at the podium with half a dozen fighters standing behind him, reasoning that journalists would be far less inclined to give such a line up a hard time. He described the idea as a bit of fun.

The offer had been made publicly a day earlier, and it was never clear how seriously it was meant, although White had said he would travel to Washington to meet the president. The episode came as the White House reshuffles its senior staff after heavy Republican losses in the midterm elections.

title: Nvidia orders independent inquiry as Trump stands by Jensen Huang
summary: The chipmaker is examining claims its chief executive was targeted by a foreign spy service, while Republicans in Congress demand answers.
body:
Nvidia has launched an independent investigation following reports that its founder and chief executive, Jensen Huang, was the target of a foreign intelligence operation.

The company announced the review on Sunday. It follows reporting last month that President Donald Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence that Mr Huang had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing. Mr Huang has since acknowledged being intimate with the woman and said he had been unfaithful to his wife, adding that he would cooperate with a security review.

Mr Trump, who relies on Mr Huang as an adviser on artificial intelligence, played the matter down when speaking to reporters. He called the Nvidia chief an honourable man who probably had an explanation, said he had not heard of any wrongdoing, and suggested he would still be glad to take him on a trip to Asia next week. He brushed aside a question about whether he regretted not acting on the intelligence when it first reached him.

Separately, it has emerged that Secretary of State Marco Rubio helped draft a confidential memo this spring flagging concerns about Mr Huang's ties to the woman linked to Chinese intelligence, showing that senior officials were worried well before the affair became public.

Republican lawmakers have taken a sharper line than the president, asking Mr Huang to give the House foreign affairs and intelligence committees a closed briefing.

The episode lands at a sensitive moment for Nvidia, whose advanced chips sit at the centre of the technology rivalry between Washington and Beijing, and for a White House that has championed the company's expansion.

title: Trump says Iran land blockade is in force as drone darkens Iraqi Kurdistan
summary: Washington's squeeze on Iran's overland supply routes has begun, the president says, while a drone strike on a gas field leaves most of northern Iraq's Kurdish region without electricity.
body:
President Donald Trump says the American economic blockade aimed at Iran's land supply routes, known as Iron Gate, is now in effect. The measure follows the creation of a task force charged with cutting off the overland corridors Tehran relies on for trade and supplies.

The president paired the announcement with a conditional offer. He said a return to American strikes on Iran was highly unlikely provided there was progress in negotiations over Tehran's nuclear programme and over reopening the Strait of Hormuz, the waterway whose closure has rattled energy markets throughout the war.

Across the border in Iraq, a drone struck the Khor Mor gas facility in the Kurdistan region, starting a fire and bringing production to a halt. The damage quickly rippled through the grid, and more than 70 per cent of the Kurdish region was left without electricity after the attack.

The outage adds to the strain on Iraq, which has already complained that outside actors are using its territory in the wider conflict, and it underlines how exposed regional energy infrastructure remains while talks between Washington and Tehran hang in the balance.

title: Trump faces only hard choices as he looks for a way out of the Iran war
summary: Every path open to the White House for ending the deeply unpopular conflict carries serious costs, but the president still has options.
body:
President Donald Trump is searching for a way to bring the war with Iran to a close, and none of the routes available to him is easy.

The conflict has become deeply unpopular at home, a point underlined by last week's midterm elections, in which Republicans suffered heavy losses and the vice president openly linked the defeat to the war. That has added pressure on the White House to find an exit.

Broadly, the choices range from pressing on with military action in the hope of forcing Tehran to give way, to accepting a negotiated settlement that would require compromise on both sides. Each carries risks: further strikes could widen the fighting and keep energy markets on edge, while a deal could be attacked as rewarding Iran.

Diplomacy is under way, with Qatar acting as the main go between and Tehran weighing proposals from Doha. Yet senior American officials describe Iran's terms as unrealistic, and Iranian leaders insist the United States must end the war on every front before they move.

For now, the president appears to be keeping several doors open at once, threatening force while saying a strong agreement would make new strikes unnecessary.

title: Justice Department weighed naming a major newspaper as conspirator in Comey leak case
summary: Prosecutors considered casting a national newspaper as a co conspirator in a leak case tied to James Comey, a step that would sharply escalate the administration's clash with the press.
body:
The US Justice Department considered naming a major American newspaper as a conspirator in a leak investigation connected to former FBI director James Comey, according to a report published on Sunday.

It is not yet clear whether prosecutors will go ahead or how such a move would be framed. Treating a news organisation as a participant in a crime, rather than as the recipient of information, would mark a dramatic escalation in the Trump administration's campaign against the media and would be likely to trigger a serious legal fight over press freedom protections.

The disclosure lands as the department prepares for intense scrutiny from a Congress about to come under Democratic control after the midterm elections, with oversight of politically charged prosecutions expected to be high on the agenda.

title: More than 50 killed in one of the bloodiest days of Yemen's war
summary: A single day of strikes and fighting left more than 50 people dead, underlining how civilians are bearing the cost since the war flared again in August.
body:
Yemen has suffered one of its deadliest 24 hour spells of the conflict, with more than 50 people reported killed as strikes and fighting swept the country.

The toll reflects how sharply the violence has risen since combat between the Houthi movement and the government backed by Saudi Arabia reignited in August, ending a long period of relative calm. Civilians have repeatedly been caught up in the bombardment and the battles on the ground.

The surge comes as the Houthis keep firing missiles towards Saudi territory, including the capital Riyadh, while a coalition led by Riyadh continues air raids on areas held by the group, among them the capital Sanaa. Government forces, meanwhile, are struggling to turn back recent Houthi advances. Aid agencies have long warned that any return to full scale war would push one of the world's poorest countries deeper into crisis.

title: Sand cliff collapses onto tents of displaced families in Gaza
summary: At least five people, children among them, have been killed after a bank of sand gave way on a camp sheltering families forced from their homes.
body:
At least five people have been killed in Gaza, among them children, after a sand cliff collapsed onto tents where displaced families had been sheltering.

Footage of the scene shows the aftermath, with makeshift shelters buried beneath the fallen sand as people search the site. The families living there had already been driven from their homes and were relying on tents for cover.

The deaths add to a grim run of days for Gaza's displaced population. The territory's first winter storm of the season has already flooded tens of thousands of tents, leaving many families without dry shelter.

The camps spread across Gaza offer little protection from the elements, and the collapse is a stark reminder of the risks faced by families with nowhere safer to go as winter sets in.

title: Native American women win a string of historic firsts in the US midterms
summary: Voters chose the first Native woman governor and senator and at least 75 Native women and gender diverse candidates across the country.
body:
Last week's US midterm elections produced a wave of historic results, and among the most striking were the gains made by Native American women.

Voters on Tuesday elected the first Native American woman to serve as a state governor and the first to sit in the US Senate, as well as the first women to lead two major tribal nations. Across the country, at least 75 Native women and gender diverse candidates won office, according to a tally by a Native political leadership group and a Native news organisation.

Deb Haaland, a citizen of Laguna Pueblo who served as interior secretary under President Joe Biden, will become governor of New Mexico. Peggy Flanagan, a member of the White Earth band of Ojibwe and currently Minnesota's lieutenant governor, won a seat in the Senate.

In tribal elections, Crystalyne Curley will become the first woman to lead the Navajo Nation, one of the largest tribes in the United States. Tina Abrams will head the Seneca Nation of Indians in western New York, the first woman to do so in the modern history of the state's biggest tribe.

There could be more to come. Mary Peltola, who is Yup'ik, holds a narrow lead in Alaska's still undecided Senate race and could join Ms Flanagan as a second Native woman in the chamber.

The results sit alongside other milestones from the same night, including the election of the country's first Muslim senator and its first Black woman governor, in a vote that handed Democrats control of Congress. Campaigners described the scale of the Native gains as a profound shift in representation for communities long absent from the corridors of power.

title: White House says it will not ease immigration raids after midterm defeat
summary: Officials insist deportation work will continue at full pace even as voters punished Republicans and some in the party urged a change of approach.
body:
The White House has said it will not loosen its immigration crackdown after last week's midterm elections, despite Republicans losing both chambers of Congress.

In a statement on Sunday, the administration said it would keep arresting and deporting people it describes as criminal undocumented migrants, and would not slow that effort. A spokeswoman, Lauren Bis, said no president had been stronger on immigration enforcement. The Department of Homeland Security echoed the line, saying its immigration agency was not backing away and would keep applying the law under President Donald Trump and Secretary Mullin.

The message lands after Mr Trump promoted Stephen Miller, the architect of his hardline border policy, to White House chief of staff on Friday. That appointment had already been read as a sign that the administration would not climb down. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials have recently been told to aim for about 2,700 arrests a day, up from an earlier target of 2,000.

Exit polls found immigration was the third most important issue for midterm voters, after the economy and the state of democracy. In Texas, a shift among Latino voters towards the Democrats helped the party lock in its congressional majorities. Large enforcement sweeps this year also prompted street protests in Chicago, Minneapolis and Los Angeles. In Minneapolis, two demonstrators, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were shot dead by immigration agents.

Some officials have told interviewers that the White House blames the election losses on the cost of living, broader economic worries and the war with Iran, rather than on its immigration campaign. Vice President JD Vance had earlier sounded more open to a tweak, writing that enforcement could focus more on businesses that hire undocumented labour. The public posture since Mr Miller's promotion has hardened instead.

Mr Trump himself said America had taken a giant step back in the vote, while promising his side would return bigger and stronger. The administration appears set to refuse concessions to the new Democratic majority and to press ahead on immigration through the remaining two years of his term.

title: Nvidia chief acknowledges relationship with a woman US officials call a Chinese spy
summary: Jensen Huang told staff he had an extramarital relationship with a business executive whom American intelligence linked to Beijing.
body:
Jensen Huang, the chief executive of the American chipmaker Nvidia, has acknowledged a personal relationship with a business executive whom United States officials concluded was working for Chinese intelligence.

Mr Huang confirmed an extramarital relationship in an internal message to employees on Sunday. The company has opened an investigation into the matter.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio had earlier warned officials about the entanglement. He played a part in drafting a secret memo on the subject, and senior figures in Washington were already concerned last spring.

American intelligence had cautioned that Mr Huang was involved with an executive recruited by China to gather information on the US company. The admission, and the inquiry that followed, add a sensitive national security question to the affairs of one of America's most valuable technology firms.

title: Iran warns it will rain down hell if the US resumes attacks
