summary: Foreign minister Abbas Araghchi ties a two day proposal to an end of fighting on all fronts, while President Trump says more strikes are unlikely if talks advance.
body:
Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, has warned that Tehran will rain down hell if the United States starts attacking again, presenting Washington with a stark choice as the two countries seek a way out of an eight month war.

In a public post on Sunday, Mr Araghchi said a two day proposal still stood. If the other side met the stated requirements, including an end to the war on all fronts, results would follow. If it chose war instead, he said, Iran's alert and battle hardened forces would rain down hell. The foreign ministry separately quoted him as saying Iran would not go easy on American targets in the region.

President Donald Trump struck a more conditional note. He said fresh strikes were highly unlikely if negotiations moved forward on Iran's nuclear programme and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. Asked whether attacks would continue, he said it depended on whether Tehran signed a very strong agreement. He added that he would go on if necessary, but that American forces had already hit Iran very hard.

Mr Trump also said the United States has three aircraft carriers in the region that are fully locked and loaded, and that 38 bridges inside Iran could be knocked down in an hour if Washington chose to do so.

The exchange came after Iran's navy said an oil tanker caught fire east of the Strait of Hormuz when it struck a naval mine. The navy claimed the ship's identification systems were switched off and that it had been travelling in a no go zone.

An adviser to the commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps aerospace force, Brigadier General Ali Belali, issued a similar warning. He said weapons had been secured for years to come, that the armed forces were ready, and that any mistake by the enemy would bring a severe response. He added that capabilities had been upgraded since earlier rounds of the war.

Mr Araghchi said talks had been delayed by last week's US midterm elections, in which Democrats took control of both houses of Congress. He said it would take time for the atmosphere to settle so that mediators could resume their visits, and that Iran would have to wait.

title: Seven killed and more than 100 hurt after trains collide south of Cairo
summary: A service bound for Fayoum struck the rear of a stationary Cairo to Aswan train in al Ayyat, sending carriages down an embankment.
body:
At least seven people were killed and more than 100 were injured on Sunday when two passenger trains collided south of Cairo, in one of Egypt's worst rail accidents in recent years.

The crash happened in the al Ayyat district of Giza province, about 30 miles from the capital, between Kafr Ammar and Al Raqqa stations. Railway officials said a train travelling from Giza to Fayoum ran into the back of a service heading from Cairo to Aswan that had stopped on the same track. Several carriages left the rails and tumbled down an embankment. Some overturned, and at least one appeared to have broken apart.

Egypt's health ministry later put the number of injured above 125. The health minister, Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, said patients were being treated for broken bones and head injuries. Hospitals in the area were placed on high alert, and more than 70 ambulances took part in the rescue. The driver of one of the trains was among the dead. The public prosecutor warned that the death toll could still rise.

President Abdel Fattah el Sisi said he was following the accident with great concern and ordered a prompt inquiry to hold anyone found negligent to account. There were immediate calls in Egypt for the transport minister to resign.

Witnesses described villagers, railway workers and first responders scrambling to reach people trapped in overturned carriages. A local resident said neighbours pulled survivors out and called for help, and that some passengers caught inside a carriage of the stationary train did not survive. Another witness said the collision happened around half past one in the afternoon local time and that six carriages overturned.

The Egyptian Red Crescent offered aid and psychological support at the scene. Emergency crews and cranes were sent to clear the wreckage. Services between Giza and Upper Egypt were suspended, and officials did not say when they would resume.

Al Ayyat was also the site of Egypt's deadliest rail disaster. In 2002 a fire on a passenger train travelling from Cairo towards southern Egypt killed more than 370 people on official figures, with some estimates higher still. Further crashes in the area in 2009 killed dozens more. Egypt's 110 million people rely heavily on the railways. The government has spent billions on roads and new high speed lines, but much of the older network has yet to be overhauled.

title: Eisenkot reaches out to Netanyahu allies as he tries to form a government
summary: The former army chief, handed 28 days to assemble a coalition, says Israel is approaching a point of no return and that his door is open.
body:
Gadi Eisenkot began the hard work of building Israel's next government on Sunday by stretching out a hand to allies of Benjamin Netanyahu, even as he accused the prime minister of leading the country into a historic crisis.

Mr Eisenkot, the 66 year old leader of the Yashar party, formally received a mandate from President Isaac Herzog at a ceremony in Jerusalem. He has 28 days to secure a majority, with a possible further 14 days if he comes close. His opposition alliance won 48 of the 120 seats in last month's election. Mr Netanyahu's camp took 53. Neither side has the 61 votes needed to govern alone.

Speaking at the president's office, Mr Eisenkot said Israel was in a state of emergency and approaching a point of no return. He called for a national emergency government and said that would take creative and unusual political steps. He said he was open to members of Likud and to Bezalel Smotrich, the far right finance minister, joining a cabinet under his leadership.

The paths in front of him are narrow: a power sharing deal with Mr Netanyahu, backing from Arab led parties, or an arrangement with the ultra Orthodox lists, which want to keep military draft exemptions for their communities. Winning over the two ultra Orthodox parties would give him exactly 61 seats. Arab led parties, which won a record 19 seats and later endorsed him, could also decide the outcome, but he has set conditions that include recognising Israel as a Jewish state and declaring Hamas a terrorist organisation. One of his partners, Yisrael Beiteinu, has already said it will not sit in a coalition with Arab led lists.

Mr Eisenkot and Mr Herzog both pointed to Israel's growing isolation after the war in Gaza and the campaign against Iran. Last week's Democratic gains in the United States have added to pressure from Israel's closest ally. Mr Eisenkot said even long standing friends were talking about reassessing their ties. Mr Herzog said Israel needed a stable government given the new political reality in Washington.

Mr Netanyahu called on Saturday night for a national unity government, though any power sharing pact would be fragile. He has claimed, without offering solid evidence, that Arab parties stole the election. If Mr Eisenkot fails, the mandate is likely to pass to Mr Netanyahu. If he too falls short, Israel could face yet another election.

title: Democrats prepare inquiries into Musk, Miller and the Trump family
summary: Incoming committee chairs say they want answers on mass federal firings, the immigration crackdown and the business affairs of the president's relatives.
body:
Democrats moving into power in Congress have begun to name the people they most want to scrutinise once they take the gavel in January, with Elon Musk and Stephen Miller high on the list.

Robert Garcia, a Democrat from California who is in line to chair the House oversight committee, said on Sunday that inquiries would look at Mr Musk's role in the mass dismissal of federal workers last year through the Department of Government Efficiency, the cost cutting body he helped to lead. Mr Garcia said there was wide interest across Congress in speaking to the world's richest man. The same committee is also expected to examine Mr Miller's part in President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown. Mr Miller is due to start work as White House chief of staff on Monday.

Jamie Raskin, who is poised to take the chair of the House judiciary committee, has asked for information on the business dealings of Jared Kushner, the president's son in law, and of Donald Trump Jr.

The planned investigations come after Mr Trump threatened Democrats who intend to oversee his administration and his family, and said he had told the Justice Department to look into them. Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Sunday that investigations were possible and claimed Republicans had faced dangerous threats, without saying what offences he believed had been committed.

The clash sets up a bitter two years in Washington, with each side promising to use the powers of office against the other after a midterm vote that handed Democrats control of both chambers.

title: Hundreds of thousands march in Amsterdam to demand action on Israel
summary: Protesters in red called for tighter trade limits and a halt to Dutch arms sales, as the prime minister defended his government's record.
body:
More than 200,000 people filled the streets of Amsterdam on Sunday in a Red Line march demanding that the Dutch government take stronger action over Israel's war in Gaza.

The Dutch branch of Amnesty International, one of the organisers, gave the crowd figure. Many marchers wore red. They called for tighter restrictions on trade with Israel and a complete stop to arms sales. A normally busy city street was closed to traffic as the column moved through. Protesters took up chants for a free Palestine. One marcher, Mike van Dongen, said what was happening in Gaza was inhumane and that the authorities, in his view, did not dare take serious steps.

Palestinian health figures put the number of people killed in Gaza since October 2023 at least 74,000, including about 21,000 children. A ceasefire came into force on 10 October last year, but Israeli attacks have continued on an almost daily basis.

Sunday's demonstration followed a similar Red Line protest in early October last year and earlier marches in The Hague in June. The war has strained ties between the Netherlands and Israel. The Dutch foreign minister resigned last year after failing to win new sanctions. A new minority coalition that took office in February then banned imports of goods from Israeli settlements, which The Hague and most of the international community regard as illegal. That step triggered a diplomatic row with Israel.

Prime Minister Rob Jetten, who joined a march last year but did not attend on Sunday, defended his record at a weekly news conference on Friday. He said his government did what it could every day to ease the suffering and that it was applying greater political and diplomatic pressure on Israel to keep its commitments on Gaza.

title: Washington voters ban foie gras as chefs prepare to fight back
summary: A ballot measure outlawing the force feeding of birds and the sale of foie gras passed easily in the US capital, helped by a campaign built around a duck.
body:
Voters in Washington DC have approved a ban on foie gras, passing a ballot measure that outlaws the force feeding of birds and the sale of the delicacy in the city.

The proposal, known as Initiative 86, won comfortably at the polls on election day. Campaigners leaned heavily on a duck named Olivia, who became the friendly face of the effort and helped turn an animal welfare question into a popular cause.

The result is not the end of the matter. Restaurant owners and some well known chefs in the capital are getting ready to challenge the measure, setting up a fresh battle over the measure. Because Congress holds unusual authority over the laws of the District, the ban could also face scrutiny beyond the city before it takes full effect.

title: Voters have turned on Trump, but two more years of his presidency remain
summary: The midterm results sent a clear message, yet America now faces a long gap between rejecting the president at the ballot box and the end of his term.
body:
The midterm elections delivered an unmistakable verdict on Donald Trump, but they have also left the country facing an uncomfortable stretch of uncertainty.

Americans have effectively signalled that they are finished with the president, handing Democrats sweeping gains in Congress. Yet Trump still has two years left in office, and nothing in the constitution shortens that time. The country must now absorb a new political reality in which a weakened president retains enormous executive power while a hostile Congress gains the tools to investigate and block him.

How that tension plays out will shape everything from immigration and trade to the war with Iran. Trump has already sent mixed signals, conceding that some policies hurt him while promoting hardline allies. For voters and allies alike, the question is whether the coming period brings compromise, confrontation or simply paralysis.

title: Jeffries says he would firmly back impeaching Pete Hegseth
summary: The Democrat expected to become House speaker says he will discuss the question with colleagues on Tuesday.
body:
Hakeem Jeffries, the Democrat widely expected to take the gavel as speaker when the new House sits in January, has said he would be a firm yes on impeaching Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Mr Jeffries said he planned to talk the matter over with fellow Democratic lawmakers on Tuesday, suggesting no formal decision has yet been made by the party.

The remark is one of the clearest signs yet of how Democrats intend to use the power they won in last week's midterm elections, which handed them control of both chambers of Congress. Party leaders have already signalled an appetite for aggressive oversight of the Trump administration.

Mr Hegseth has been one of the most contested figures in the cabinet. The White House has recently denied reports that he is preparing to leave his post.

An impeachment in the House would require only a simple majority, but removal from office would need a two thirds vote in the Senate, a bar that remains far out of reach.

title: Iran war oil shock drives both electric cars and a dash for fossil fuels
summary: Soaring crude prices have lifted demand for electric vehicles while pushing governments to lock in secure power supplies of any kind.
body:
The surge in oil prices caused by the Iran war is pulling the global energy system in two directions at once, as the world's climate negotiators gather for this year's UN summit.

On one side, the shock has fuelled a jump in demand for electric vehicles, as drivers and companies look for ways to escape volatile fuel costs. On the other, it has set off a race among governments to secure reliable power quickly, which in many cases means leaning harder on fossil fuels.

The disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important routes for crude and gas, has made energy security a top priority in capitals across Asia and Europe.

The split creates a difficult backdrop for climate talks, where delegates are trying to keep pressure on countries to cut emissions while many of them are scrambling to keep the lights on and costs down at home.

title: Peltola holds a narrow lead in Alaska as Trump insists Republicans won
summary: The Democratic challenger is about 600 votes ahead of Senator Dan Sullivan with a quarter of ballots still to count.
body:
President Donald Trump is continuing to claim victory for Republicans in Alaska's Senate race even though counting is far from over and the Democrat is narrowly in front.

Mary Peltola, the Democratic challenger, leads the Republican incumbent, Senator Dan Sullivan, by roughly 600 votes, according to tallies compiled by a US news agency. About a quarter of all ballots have still to be counted.

Alaska is known for slow counts, in part because of its vast distances and the time allowed for postal votes to arrive, so final results in close contests often take days or weeks.

The race is among a handful still too close to call after a midterm election in which Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. A Peltola win would add to the scale of the Republican defeat and deepen questions over the president's hold on voters.

Until every remaining ballot is counted, neither side can claim the seat, whatever the president says.

title: Iran executes three men accused of unrest during January protests
summary: State media said Hassan Dioband, Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh were convicted over violence in Karaj after nationwide demonstrations.
body:
Iran has executed three men accused of taking part in armed unrest during the anti government protests that swept the country in January, state media reported.

Hassan Dioband, Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh were said to have thrown firebombs and grenades, used knives and guns, and set fire to public buildings in Karaj, a city west of Tehran. Officials also linked them to damage at an electricity substation that caused local power cuts. State media said the Supreme Court upheld their convictions and found them guilty of acting on behalf of Israel, the United States and hostile groups.

Mr Dioband was arrested on 11 January after investigators named him as a suspect in attacks on public property and in incitement. Ten other people accused of taking part in unrest under his direction were later detained and received prison terms of five to ten years.

The protest movement began in December last year over the cost of living and grew into nationwide demonstrations against the government, peaking on 8 and 9 January. Iranian authorities said more than 3,000 people died and blamed the bloodshed on terrorist acts they said were orchestrated by Washington and Israel. Groups based outside the country published higher death tolls, and there were multiple accounts of security forces firing on unarmed demonstrators.

The three hangings are the latest in a series tied to the protests, including cases in which defendants were accused of links to Israel and the United States. Executions have risen since American and Israeli strikes on Iran began in late February.

Volker Türk, the United Nations human rights chief, has said he is alarmed by the increase. In August he reported that at least 56 people had been put to death on national security charges since 19 March, 27 of them in cases connected to the January unrest.

Iran is widely regarded as the world's second most frequent user of the death penalty, after China. Amnesty International said the country executed at least 2,159 people last year, the highest total recorded since 1981, including 45 suspected dissidents condemned on national security charges.

title: Egypt reopens its Tripoli embassy after 12 years in a shift on Libya
summary: Cairo's return to the Libyan capital is being read by analysts as a recalibration of its long standing support for the eastern camp led by Khalifa Haftar.
body:
Egypt has reopened its embassy in Tripoli for the first time in 12 years, a step analysts in the region describe as a turning point in how Cairo deals with its divided western neighbour.

Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty opened the building on Saturday. The mission had been shut for security reasons for more than a decade, and no Egyptian foreign minister had visited the Libyan capital in five years.

Libya has been split since the overthrow of Muammar Gaddafi in 2011. One administration sits in Tripoli in the west, while a rival authority holds sway in Tobruk and Benghazi in the east. Thousands have died in fighting between militias loyal to the competing camps.

For years Egypt was seen as the main regional patron of the eastern side, dominated by the military commander Khalifa Haftar and his Libyan National Army. Tripoli, by contrast, was the seat of the internationally recognised government that Haftar's forces once tried to seize.

Libyan analysts say the move goes beyond restoring consular services. In their view it signals that Cairo is rearranging its priorities and wants working ties with every Libyan faction rather than one.

The change sits within a wider realignment. In July, Turkey and the eastern forces reached an unusual level of cooperation, including plans for military facilities, surveillance systems and training in Turkey for eastern officers. Haftar's son Saddam, deputy commander of the eastern forces, has also visited Ankara and Doha, both of which backed the Tripoli government in the past.

Inside Libya, the rival sides have signed a deal known as the 4+4 agreement, which sets out a path towards presidential and parliamentary elections over the next two years. Supporters hope it can lead to a unity government and an end to years of conflict.

title: Debris from intercepted Houthi missile damages Aramco tower in Riyadh
summary: Saudi officials say a building in the capital's financial district was struck by falling fragments after a missile from Yemen was shot down, with no injuries reported.
body:
A tower belonging to Saudi Aramco in the financial district of Riyadh was damaged on Sunday after Yemen's Houthi movement fired missiles towards the Saudi capital.

Saudi authorities said the building was hit by fragments that fell after air defences intercepted an incoming missile. They reported that nobody was hurt.

The incident brings the Yemen conflict closer to the heart of the kingdom's economy. The state oil giant is the country's most valuable company, and the district where its tower stands is home to banks, ministries and corporate offices.

It comes as fighting between the Houthis and Yemen's Saudi backed government continues to escalate, with a sharp rise in strikes and casualties in recent days. The Houthis have repeatedly launched missiles and drones at Saudi territory, while the Saudi led coalition has carried out air raids on areas the group controls.

Officials gave no estimate of the cost of the damage, and there was no immediate word on how many missiles were fired in the latest attack.

title: Data centre boom fuels a surge in US fossil fuel pipeline projects
summary: A review of federal records finds nearly 200 new or planned pipelines, even as safety rules are loosened and enforcement drops.
body:
A rush to build data centres across the United States is helping to drive the largest pipeline building boom in decades, according to a review of federal records, just as the Trump administration rolls back rules meant to limit accidents and pollution.

The Environmental Integrity Project found almost 200 pipeline schemes that are proposed or already under way. Together they would run for about 17,000 miles. Many are meant to feed gas fired power stations planned for data centres. The researchers counted at least 98 such plants. If every line were completed, the network would move about 40 percent more natural gas each day than it does now. The same review said pipelines are also being laid to support gas exports linked to the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

Most of the projects would carry gas through 42 states, with clusters in producing regions. About 42 lines are in or cross Texas, 27 are in Louisiana, and nine each are in Pennsylvania and Illinois. More than a quarter of the schemes have asked for a faster environmental review. The administration has used tools such as an energy emergency declaration and the Defense Production Act to speed permits, sometimes over the objections of states.

The group warned that this burst of construction coincides with a drive to weaken environmental and safety protections. The administration has said it will not bring enforcement cases against firms that breach pipeline safety rules. By last year the average number of enforcement actions had already been cut in half, to 117. Officials have also allowed higher operating pressures in densely populated areas and fewer pressure tests.

The United States already records about 1.7 pipeline accidents, spills, fires or explosions each day. In March 2023 a cracked gas line in West Reading, Pennsylvania, set off a blast at a chocolate factory that killed seven workers and injured ten. Last month two workers died when a pipeline exploded in New Mexico.

The new lines could also damage more than 19,000 acres of federally protected wetlands, the review found, while the administration tries to strip protection from the great majority of such sites. Communities in southwest Louisiana, where many export terminals already cut through marshes and fishing grounds, say they would bear the risk while the profits flow elsewhere.

title: Russian strikes cut power to about 850,000 people in eastern Ukraine
summary: Overnight attacks on energy sites in the Dnipropetrovsk and Kharkiv regions plunged hundreds of thousands into darkness days before new peace talks.
body:
Around 850,000 people in eastern Ukraine lost electricity on Sunday after Russian forces struck energy infrastructure overnight, according to Ukrainian officials and the country's largest private power company.

The bulk of the outages hit the Dnipropetrovsk region, where more than 600,000 customers were cut off. Homes and businesses in the city of Dnipro and the Pavlohrad, Samarivskyi and Kamianske districts were all affected. The energy firm said crews had reached the damaged facility but that further attacks were slowing the repair work.

A separate strike on an infrastructure site in the Kharkiv region in the northeast left roughly 250,000 more people without power. A local mayor said there were no casualties but could not say when supplies would be restored.

The latest blows came only a day after Ukraine's energy ministry reported a large scale attack that blacked out parts of five regions and disrupted transmission in Kyiv.

Ukraine is preparing for another bitter wartime winter as Russia steps up near daily barrages of drones and missiles aimed at the grid. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Moscow of escalating the strikes to squeeze his government ahead of US brokered three way talks due on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Russia's defence ministry said its forces would keep targeting Ukrainian fuel and energy sites, which it claims are used to support the Ukrainian military.

title: Democrats put healthcare and tariffs first, not impeachment, after midterm win
summary: Fresh from regaining power in Congress, Democrats are expected to pair tough investigations of the Trump administration with a lawmaking push on living costs.
body:
Democrats are mapping out how to use their new strength in Congress after Tuesday's midterm elections handed them a sweeping return to power and real leverage over President Donald Trump.

For close to two years the party hammered the administration on three broad themes: the cost of living, chaos in government and corruption. Voters appear to have rewarded that message, and attention has now turned to what Democrats will actually do with their majorities.

The early signs point to an agenda built around healthcare and tariffs, two issues that touch household budgets directly. Party figures are also expected to launch demanding investigations into the conduct of the administration, using the oversight powers that come with control of congressional committees.

Impeaching the president, however, does not appear to be on the immediate menu. Leaders seem wary of a drawn out fight that could distract from pocketbook issues ahead of the 2028 presidential race.

The coming two years are likely to see a mix of hard bargaining with the White House and open confrontation, as both sides test the limits of divided government.

title: Stimulant overdoses climb across the US even as opioid deaths fall
summary: Federal health data show more overdoses involving stimulants, and doctors say these cases are harder to spot and to treat than opioid emergencies.
body:
Overdoses linked to stimulants are rising in many parts of the United States, according to recent figures from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, even as deaths from opioids continue to come down.

Public awareness of opioid overdoses has grown sharply in recent years, helped by campaigns that taught people how to recognise the signs and use reversal medicine. Experts say there has been no comparable effort for stimulants such as methamphetamine and cocaine, whose overdoses can look very different and have no single antidote.

A physician in Sacramento who works in emergency and addiction medicine said the fall in overdoses in California had been far smaller than expected, partly because of the stimulant problem.

Doctors say responding to these emergencies is more complicated, since symptoms can include dangerous heart strain, overheating and agitation that require hospital care rather than a quick fix at the scene. They are calling for clearer public education and better treatment options as the pattern of drug harm in the country shifts.

title: Justice Department prepares for wave of oversight as Democrats take Congress
summary: Democrats have vowed to examine how the department has been run during Trump's second term, while the president has told it to investigate them.
body:
The US Justice Department is bracing for intense scrutiny from Capitol Hill after Democrats swept last week's midterm elections and won control of Congress.

Democratic lawmakers have promised to look closely at the department's actions during President Donald Trump's second term, including decisions they see as politically driven. Control of committees will give them the power to call officials to testify, demand documents and hold public hearings.

The prospect sets up a clash between the two branches. Trump has already ordered the department to open inquiries into Democrats, a move his critics describe as an attempt to turn law enforcement against political opponents.

Officials inside the department are expected to face a heavy load of requests and hearings in the months ahead, as the new majority makes oversight of federal law enforcement one of its early priorities.

title: Yemen government struggles to reverse Houthi gains despite Saudi air power
summary: Efforts to roll back the Houthi offensive appear to have stalled, leaving civilians increasingly trapped between the warring sides.
body:
The drive by Yemen's internationally recognised government to push back a recent Houthi offensive appears to have lost momentum, according to a fresh assessment of the fighting.

Saudi Arabia, which leads the coalition backing the government, has thrown its air force into the battle, but air strikes alone have so far not been enough to turn the tide on the ground. Government forces have struggled to retake territory seized by the Houthis since fighting flared again in August.

The stalemate has come at a heavy cost for ordinary Yemenis. Civilians living near the front lines and in cities hit by strikes find themselves increasingly caught between the two sides, with little chance of escape and few places considered safe.

The conflict has grown more intense in recent days, with deadly strikes reported around the capital, Sanaa, and continued clashes on several fronts. Neither side appears close to a decisive breakthrough, raising fears of a long and bloody new chapter in a war that had been relatively quiet for much of the past few years.

title: Is West Bank settler violence state policy or fringe extremism?
summary: As settler attacks wear away Palestinian self rule, the debate over who is responsible turns to whether a new Israeli leader could change course.
body:
The surge in attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank has sparked a sharp argument inside and outside Israel over who is really to blame.

Supporters of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu tend to describe the violence as the work of a radical fringe, including troubled teenagers acting outside the law. Critics reject that picture. They argue that government policy and public money have helped to create the conditions for the attacks, and some go as far as calling it a form of state violence.

Whatever the cause, the effect on the ground has been to steadily weaken the limited self rule that Palestinians exercise in parts of the territory.

The question has taken on new weight now that Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief, has been asked to try to form Israel's next government after an inconclusive election. Some Palestinians and Israeli critics of the settler movement hope he may take a firmer line, though it remains unclear what a coalition led by him could agree on, or whether he will manage to build one at all.

title: Possible 2028 rivals to Vance start preparing after heavy Republican losses
summary: The vice president has not decided on a White House run, but would be challengers are already moving after a bruising midterm night for the party.
body:
Republicans who may want the party's presidential nomination in 2028 are beginning to position themselves after the party suffered painful defeats in the midterm elections.

Vice President JD Vance has long been seen as the natural heir to Donald Trump, but he has not yet made up his mind about running. His potential rivals, sensing that the scale of the losses has weakened any claim to automatic succession, are wasting little time in laying the groundwork for their own campaigns.

The results have prompted a wider debate inside the party about whether to stay loyal to the Trump brand or chart a different course. That argument is likely to shape an increasingly open contest, with several figures testing support among donors and activists well before any formal announcements.

Members of both parties have suggested that a crowded and competitive primary season could ultimately be healthy, forcing candidates and their ideas to face real scrutiny.

title: Kyiv weighs whether a Democratic Congress will change its war with Russia
summary: Ukrainian officials and analysts see a possible boost from the US midterm result, while soldiers at the front say they have learned to rely less on Washington.
body:
The Democratic sweep in this week's US midterm elections has raised hopes in Kyiv of firmer American backing, though many Ukrainians, including those fighting, say they no longer count on Washington.

A wounded drone technician recovering in a Kyiv hospital said the result meant little to him, arguing that Ukraine had learned to stand on its own and that demand for its drones was now global.

American support has shrunk sharply under President Donald Trump. Close to $200bn in financial and military aid flowed from the start of Russia's full scale invasion in 2022 to late 2024, but the stream has slowed to a trickle since 2025. Between October 2025 and March, Ukraine received about $8.2bn in military aid through programmes left over from the previous administration.

Europe has taken on most of the financial burden, providing $83bn in 2025 alone, yet a German research institute estimates that close to a third of the weapons Ukraine receives still come from US companies.

Democrats, who take control of both chambers on 3 January, have promised to examine Mr Trump's dealings with Russia and to investigate alleged corruption linked to his family, including reported ties to Russian figures. They have signalled they are ready to issue subpoenas and demand executive branch records, among them documents on Ukraine.

A Kyiv based political analyst said Ukraine's position could strengthen, but stressed the importance of keeping support from both parties. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy struck a similar tone, saying Ukraine enjoys backing across the aisle and thanking Republicans as well as Democrats.

title: Storm floods 70,000 tents across Gaza as displaced families lose shelter
summary: Heavy rain and gales since Friday have soaked or destroyed tens of thousands of makeshift shelters, with rescuers fielding more than 1,500 emergency calls.
body:
A storm that swept across the Gaza Strip from late Friday has left tens of thousands of displaced Palestinians without dry shelter, according to local authorities, as heavy rain and strong winds tore through the tents that have become home for much of the population.

Gaza's Government Media Office said about 70,000 tents were flooded and dozens of walls collapsed during the bad weather. It put the cost of the damage at roughly three million dollars, a figure that does little to capture the scale of loss for families who had already been uprooted several times.

The Civil Defence service said it had answered at least 1,500 emergency calls. It warned that more than 2,000 buildings were now at risk of falling down and estimated that around 300,000 tents would be needed to give people affected by the weather adequate cover.

Reporters in Gaza City described rows of soaked mattresses, bedding and clothing, and said families had spent days trying to strengthen their shelters only to see them ripped apart within hours. Close to 400,000 displaced people are thought to be living in sites judged highly exposed to further flooding.

In Deir el Balah, in the centre of the territory, families whose tents were swamped said they had received no food aid since early Saturday.

A senior UNICEF official in the Palestinian territories said most people were living in dreadful conditions and appealed for more funding so that agencies could deliver urgently needed help.

The storm has hit a population already in deep humanitarian distress. Israel continues to place tight limits on aid, shelter materials and reconstruction supplies entering the strip, and relief groups say those restrictions have made it hard to prepare for winter.

The war that began in October 2023 has wrecked much of Gaza's housing and infrastructure. Local health authorities say more than 74,640 people have been killed since then, including at least 1,610 since a truce took effect in October 2025.

title: Freed Palestinian prisoners in the West Bank face repeated arrests and raids
summary: Hundreds of former detainees say Israeli forces keep raiding their homes, holding them for hours and threatening to send them back to jail.
body:
Palestinians released from Israeli prisons into the occupied West Bank say their freedom is largely in name only, as Israeli forces repeatedly raid their homes, detain them for hours and summon them for questioning.

Groups that monitor prisoners' affairs record dozens of arrests across the territory every day, many of them in sweeping operations that often single out people who have served time before. Most are let go after several hours of interrogation, a pattern that rights workers see as a deliberate campaign of intimidation aimed at former prisoners and their families.

One man, 43, who asked to be identified only by a pseudonym because he fears being arrested again, was freed in January 2025 under an exchange agreement between Hamas and Israel after spending 22 years of a life term behind bars.

Within days of his release, he says, Israeli intelligence officers called him in and told him they disagreed with the political decision to free him, warning that any small misstep would land him back in a cell. Since then he has been arrested six times and summoned five more times for questioning. On each occasion soldiers searched his home, and his father was once detained simply because his son was standing outside the house at night.

He described being made to walk several kilometres in handcuffs and a blindfold, then held in poor conditions without food or water, beaten and insulted before being threatened with a return to prison. He said he now feels that most of him is still locked up.

His family, he said, stays awake whenever there are reports of troops in the city, and some neighbours leave their own homes for fear of being caught up in raids linked to him.

Hundreds of other former prisoners describe similar experiences, with some saying their homes are searched as often as twice a week. Their accounts come as Israeli military operations across the West Bank continue at a high tempo.

title: Saudi air defences down Houthi missiles fired at Riyadh and the Eastern Province
summary: The Saudi led coalition says it destroyed several ballistic and cruise missiles aimed at the kingdom, as Houthi officials report dozens killed in coalition raids near Sanaa.
body:
Saudi Arabia's air defences intercepted a fresh wave of Houthi missiles on Sunday, according to the Saudi led coalition fighting the group in Yemen. Coalition spokesman Major General Turki al Maliki said three ballistic missiles had been destroyed, two of them heading for Riyadh. A further ballistic missile aimed at the Eastern Province was also brought down, he said.

Later in the day the coalition reported that two cruise missiles had been intercepted over Riyadh and the south of the country. No damage or casualties inside the kingdom were reported.

The launches came hours after the Houthi run health ministry said coalition air raids on the village of al Shariyah, in the Bani Hushaish district east of Sanaa, had killed 33 people on Saturday. Its spokesman said eight women and 13 children were among the dead and at least 39 others were wounded, adding that homes, roads and rescue crews had been hit. The coalition did not immediately respond to the claim, and it could not be independently confirmed.

The Houthis' military spokesman claimed the coalition had carried out more than a hundred air and missile strikes across Sanaa and seven other provinces in a single day. He also said Houthi forces had mounted six attacks of their own on Aramco oil sites, Riyadh airport and Saudi military positions along the border.

The escalation follows a deadly strike on a market in Taiz province on Friday that killed 30 people, with each side blaming the other. Government forces launched a campaign last month to retake Houthi held territory, including the capital.

United Nations figures put the death toll at more than 1,600, with nearly 300,000 people displaced, since a 2022 truce broke down in July when the Houthis declared a blockade of Saudi ports.

title: Satellites and rockets become a new battleground in the Russia Ukraine war
summary: Ukrainian strikes on Russian space industry sites, Moscow's push for its own satellite network and orbital harassment show how the war has spread beyond the earth.
body:
The war between Russia and Ukraine is increasingly being fought over access to space, as both sides race to secure the satellites that guide drones, sensors and communications on the battlefield.

In the early hours of 15 August, Ukrainian missiles struck the Progress Rocket and Space Centre in the Volga city of Samara, the maker of Russia's Soyuz rockets. Two buildings were hit, among them a clean room where circuit boards for the launch systems were assembled. The factory builds the rockets that carry Russia's new Rassvet satellites, a network Moscow is rushing into orbit after it was cut off from Elon Musk's Starlink earlier this year.

Ukraine has also struck other sites linked to the Russian space agency this year, including the Korolyov complex north of Moscow and a radio telescope in occupied Crimea that was originally built by Ukraine.

Russia, for its part, has fired its Oreshnik ballistic missile at least three times. The weapon climbs to the edge of space before releasing several warheads that can strike separate targets. That threat, together with recent limits on Starlink service, has pushed Kyiv to reduce its reliance on American systems. Ukraine has run at least three tests of interceptions at very high altitude, and last month it launched a first test satellite with a Danish partner for a planned national communications network that could eventually number about 245 satellites.

Tensions in orbit are rising more widely. In September the US air force secretary acknowledged for the first time that Washington had placed space control weapons in orbit. Weeks later a Russian satellite was seen manoeuvring aggressively towards a commercial Finnish radar satellite that supplies terrain imaging to Ukraine's military, a move experts described as deliberate harassment that could force the target to burn scarce fuel.

Specialists say the treaties meant to govern space are vague, dated and hard to enforce. One Swedish defence academic argued that warfare in orbit is no longer a distant prospect but a present reality.

title: Zelenskyy says North Korean missiles were used in a fresh barrage on Ukraine
summary: An overnight wave of drones and ballistic missiles cut power in several regions as Kyiv prepares for talks in Abu Dhabi and asks Washington for more air defences.
body:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of stepping up attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure in order to squeeze Kyiv before talks due this week, and said the latest barrage included ballistic missiles made in North Korea.

Ukraine's energy ministry said a large assault on Saturday on several energy sites plunged five regions into darkness and badly disrupted electricity supplies in Kyiv and nearby areas. Zelenskyy said Russia had launched 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles overnight, among them KN 23 missiles manufactured and supplied by North Korea. He argued that Moscow treats diplomacy as another form of aggression and is trying to weaken Ukraine's position, and that of its partners, before negotiations begin.

Those talks are planned as a United States brokered meeting in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, the first such three way encounter in months. Ukrainian officials are expected to sit down with Russian negotiators and American envoys. Diplomacy has been largely stalled since February, when Washington turned much of its attention to the war with Iran.

Zelenskyy also appealed for more American help, saying Ukraine still lacks enough interceptor missiles for Patriot air defence batteries and that the United States is best placed to fill the gap.

Russia reported its own losses from Ukrainian drones. Officials in the Belgorod region said one person was killed when a drone hit a private house in the town of Grayvoron. The Russian defence ministry said its forces shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight across ten regions, as well as over Crimea and the Black and Azov seas. Russian media later said the Saratov oil refinery had been struck and published pictures of smoke rising over the city.

In Italy, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said pro Russian hackers had published his personal data on the dark web after he backed Ukraine, and were offering to pay for further details about him and his family. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called the trade in private information about public officials a serious concern. Moscow has not commented.

title: Houthi authorities say Sanaa air strikes killed at least 33 people
summary: Outlets aligned with the movement say women and children were among the dead in a village east of the capital, while Saudi Arabia and its coalition partners have offered no comment.
body:
Houthi aligned media in Yemen say at least 33 people were killed when air strikes hit al Shariyah, a town east of Sanaa, on Saturday. Officials named women and children among the dead and said 39 people were wounded.

Video from a television station run by the movement showed rescuers lifting bodies, including those of young children, from the ruins of several buildings, and injured people being carried to hospital on stretchers. A Houthi run news agency said Saudi Arabia carried out the raid. The Saudi led coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognised government has not responded.

The figures mark a rise on earlier local counts from the same attack, which had put the death toll in the mid twenties. Hours before the bombs fell on al Shariyah, the coalition said it had intercepted a missile heading towards Riyadh. Mahdi al Mashat, who heads the Houthi political leadership, pledged that the movement would take revenge.

The wider war had been largely frozen for years before the conflict with Iran brought it back to life. A fragile pause began to collapse after Saudi forces struck Sanaa airport, which the Houthis control, to stop an Iranian aircraft from landing. The Houthis then attacked Abha airport inside Saudi Arabia and later targeted Saudi ships using the Red Sea as an alternative oil export route while the Strait of Hormuz remained disrupted.

Fighting between the Houthis and forces loyal to the Saudi backed government has since resumed in earnest. On Friday a market in Taiz province, one of the main battlegrounds of recent weeks, was hit in an attack said to have killed about 30 people. Each side blamed the other, the Houthis accusing Saudi aircraft and government forces saying a Houthi missile was responsible.

The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since combat flared again.

title: Washington sets up a task force to choke Iran's overland supply routes
summary: US Central Command says a new unit will work to stop weapons, sanctioned goods and illicit money moving across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea, widening its naval blockade.
body:
The United States has opened a new front in its pressure campaign on Iran, announcing a task force designed to cut the country's overland supply lines. US Central Command said on Saturday that the unit, named Task Force Iron Gate, would build on what it called the success of its naval blockade of Iranian ports.

The force will be run from Tampa in Florida and will work alongside other US government agencies. Its brief is to stop advanced weapons, sensitive technology, sanctioned materials and illicit revenue from crossing Iran's land frontiers and the Caspian Sea, according to the command.

A former senior Pentagon official for the Middle East said the unit would map where weapons enter Iran, how those routes might be severed and how Tehran moves its energy exports. He suggested that if President Donald Trump chose to escalate the war, the next wave of targets could be economic and infrastructure sites rather than purely military ones, as part of a wider effort to cut off the government's ability to fight and to pay for the war.

On the same day, Central Command said a US military aircraft had fired on the stern of the cargo ship Huda in the Gulf of Oman after its crew was told to leave the targeted areas, leaving the vessel disabled. The command said 147 commercial ships had turned back in compliance since July, while five that refused had been disabled.

Iranian state media reported two explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday and several more in Jask, Sirik and Bandar Abbas. Mr Trump had confirmed new strikes on Qeshm a day earlier but described them as minor, saying Tehran still wanted a deal as talks mediated by Qatar continue.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard navy separately said two oil tankers had struck mines near the strait after sailing through an unsafe stretch with navigation systems switched off, leaving both badly damaged.

title: UAE rescuers save 22 sailors as blasts and mines shake waters near Hormuz
summary: Coast guard teams pulled Arab crew from a burning cargo ship in the Sea of Oman, while Iran reported explosions along its southern coast and two tankers hitting mines.
body:
The UAE National Guard said on Sunday that its coast guard had rescued 22 crew members after a fire broke out on a cargo ship in the Sea of Oman.

According to the guard, the ship's crew reported the blaze and specialist teams found the vessel, reached it and took everyone off. The sailors, all of them Arab nationals, were given first aid and handed to the relevant authorities. All 22 were said to be in a stable condition. The cause of the fire was not made clear.

The rescue came as Iran reported a tense day on and around the Strait of Hormuz. The navy of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said two oil tankers had struck mines on Saturday after passing through an unsafe stretch of the strait with their navigation systems switched off. Iranian state television said the ships suffered severe damage and came to a halt.

Iran's official news agency also reported the sound of two explosions on Qeshm Island, which sits in the strait, and several more blasts in the coastal cities of Jask, Sirik and Bandar Abbas. A day earlier President Donald Trump said United States forces had carried out new strikes on Qeshm, describing them as minor, while also saying Tehran still wanted a deal. Talks mediated by Qatar are continuing.

In a separate enforcement action in the Gulf of Oman, United States Central Command said a military aircraft had fired precision munitions at the stern of the Huda, a commercial cargo ship flagged in St Kitts, after the crew were told to leave targeted parts of the vessel. The command said the ship was disabled as part of the naval blockade of Iranian ports. It added that since July its forces had redirected 147 commercial vessels that complied with instructions and disabled five merchant ships that did not.

Washington also said it was stepping up efforts to block land routes used to move weapons and other goods alongside the months long blockade at sea.

title: Republicans search for a path after the midterm collapse of the Trump coalition
summary: Party figures are split between doubling down on the president and looking beyond him, as voting data show steep losses among Latino and younger supporters.
body:
Republicans are arguing over what comes next after the voting alliance that carried Donald Trump to three presidential nominations broke apart in the 2026 midterms.

The party lost the House and the Senate, and also surrendered governorships and legislatures in states such as Texas and Kansas, places where Trump himself had won by wide margins. Ron DeSantis, the outgoing governor of Florida, called the result close to an extinction level event for Republicans. Vice President JD Vance blamed public anger over the war with Iran and said a period of infighting was inevitable, while arguing that the party could still recover.

Over the past decade most Republicans have moved right on immigration and turned away from the interventionist foreign policy associated with the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. The more moderate wing of the party in Congress has almost vanished. This year even long serving figures who had clashed with Trump, including John Cornyn in Texas and Susan Collins in Maine, lost their seats.

Three days after the vote Trump named Stephen Miller, the architect of his hardline immigration policy, as White House chief of staff in place of Susie Wiles, a sign that he does not intend to soften his approach. Steve Bannon, a leading voice of the Maga movement, predicted a civil war inside the party, blamed the economy and foreign wars for the defeat, and urged Trump to intensify mass deportations. Another strategist argued that loyal Trump voters remain numerous but that a non Maga majority now exists inside the party.

An analysis of voter data found that Latino support for Democratic candidates rose by 29 percentage points between 2024 and 2026, while support among voters aged 18 to 29 rose by 33 points. Those swings match polling that showed deep discontent with Trump's record on prices, immigration and the Iran war, as well as a sense that he was more interested in building projects such as a White House ballroom than in living costs.

Before the midterms Vance was widely seen as the favourite for the Republican presidential nomination in 2028. Strategists now say that race is wide open. Other names mentioned include Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz, DeSantis, Nikki Haley and Chris Christie. Trump's endorsement, if he offers one, is likely to weigh heavily.

title: Trump asks the UFC chief to become White House press secretary
summary: Dana White says he will fly to Washington for a meeting on Monday after a public job offer that also asked him to bring fighters into the briefing room.
body:
President Donald Trump has publicly asked Dana White, the chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, to become White House press secretary, days after Republicans lost both houses of Congress.

In a Saturday social media post, Trump said White would be unlike any previous holder of the role, described him as a fighter and a warrior, and appealed to him to take the job. He also asked White to bring six well known UFC athletes to serve as aides, even though some are not American, saying they were needed to stand up to the left. The fighters he named included Islam Makhachev and Khabib Nurmagomedov, both from a Muslim majority region of Russia, as well as Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes and Kayla Harrison, whose surname he misspelled.

The post came with pictures, including an image that appeared to show White at the briefing room lectern. White later shared a similar picture of himself in that room with a caption about starting the next chapter. Some reports then said he had turned the idea down and that an aide to the president had treated it as a joke.

White was in London on Saturday night for a boxing card. Asked about the offer afterwards, he said he was already flying to Washington and would meet Trump on Monday, without saying whether he would accept. He noted that he already holds several jobs. Besides running the UFC he leads a slap fighting promotion, has launched a boxing company, and last year joined the board of Meta, the owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. His fortune from the fight business has been estimated at more than $600 million, far above the roughly $195,000 salary of the press secretary post.

The job has been empty since mid October, when Katie Zacharia left after fewer than five days. She had succeeded Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down at the end of August.

White is a longtime friend and political ally of Trump. He has credited the president with helping to keep the UFC alive by hosting early events at a casino in Atlantic City, spoke at Republican conventions, and appeared at Trump's 2024 victory night. This summer the UFC staged a fight event at the White House. The administration's communications director, a former UFC spokesman, publicly urged White to say yes.

title: Wisconsin state trooper detained by immigration agents is released
summary: Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, a South African officer who has waited seven years for an asylum hearing, left custody but remains under electronic monitoring.
body:
A Wisconsin state patrol trooper who was detained by federal immigration agents at an airport has been released from custody, his lawyers said.

Agents approached Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, a South African national, on Thursday as he waited to board a domestic flight. He moved to the United States at the age of 14 and has been waiting seven years for his asylum case to be heard. In the meantime he received permission to work, valid through 2030, and used it to serve in Wisconsin law enforcement.

The Department of Homeland Security defended the arrest, saying he had overstayed a visa issued in 2019 and that work permission or a pending application does not by itself confer legal status. His lawyers rejected that account, pointing out that another branch of the same department, the agency that handles citizenship and immigration services, had authorised him to work.

His legal team said on Friday that he would be freed but would have to wear an electronic monitor and check in regularly with immigration authorities. They welcomed the release while stressing that he must still argue his case before an immigration judge. The department did not immediately explain what prompted the decision to let him go.

Video from his graduation last year showed his father pinning on his badge in front of Wisconsin's governor. Van Der Merwe's family, who are white South Africans, arrived during Donald Trump's first term. After Trump returned to office they had reason to hope their claim would be viewed favourably, because the president signed an order saying the United States would promote the resettlement of Afrikaner refugees, citing claims of race based discrimination at home.

The arrest fits a wider pattern in which travellers with visas, residence papers or pending asylum cases have been stopped at airports as the administration pursues a mass deportation drive. Van Der Merwe's lawyers advised other noncitizens with unfinished immigration files to speak to an attorney before flying, even if they have travelled without trouble in the past.

title: Senator Ron Johnson accuses Trump aides of serving special interests
summary: The Wisconsin Republican used a popular podcast appearance to allege corruption inside the administration, citing claims by a former White House adviser.
body:
Ron Johnson, the Republican senator from Wisconsin and a longtime ally of President Donald Trump, has accused members of the administration of corruption.

Speaking on one of America's most popular podcasts, Mr Johnson said people around the president were catering to special interests. He based part of his criticism on allegations made by a former adviser in the White House.

The attack is striking because it comes from within the president's own party and from a senator who has generally stood by him. It follows a heavy defeat for Republicans in the midterm elections, which handed Democrats control of both the House and the Senate and set off a scramble inside the party over who and what was to blame.

Democrats have already promised wide ranging investigations of the administration once the new Congress sits in January. Criticism from Republicans such as Mr Johnson could make it harder for the White House to dismiss those inquiries as purely partisan.

title: America switches on its first digital air traffic control towers
summary: Small airports in Florida and Alaska are now guided with camera based systems, as the Trump administration pushes a costly overhaul of ageing aviation equipment.
body:
The United States has brought its first digital air traffic control towers into service, starting with two small regional airports. The Federal Aviation Administration said the systems are now running at Bartow Executive Airport in Florida and Kenai Municipal Airport in Alaska, with five more regional airports next in line.

Instead of relying only on controllers looking out of a tall glass cab, the new towers use banks of cameras and digital screens that give staff an unbroken all round view of runways, taxiways and nearby airspace. The agency insists the technology is meant to support controllers rather than replace them, giving them more information and better visibility to make safety decisions. Its administrator, Bryan Bedford, said controllers would keep doing the vital work of keeping aircraft apart, now with better tools.

Mr Bedford is due before the House transportation and infrastructure committee next week, where lawmakers are expected to press him on the progress of a $12.5bn modernisation programme. Congress approved that sum over five years in June 2025 to replace outdated kit still found across the system, from copper phone lines to floppy disks and paper strips used to track flights. The administration is now asking for a further $30bn.

The rollout comes amid wider unease over new technology in air traffic control, including an artificial intelligence tool for managing routes that the agency introduced in September. The White House has also faced criticism over a national shortage of controllers that worsened after last year's government shutdown.

Scrutiny of tower staffing has been intense since a passenger jet and a military helicopter collided near Washington in 2025, killing 67 people. It was the deadliest American air disaster in more than two decades, and investigators later concluded it could have been entirely prevented.

title: Herzog hands Eisenkot the first chance to replace Netanyahu
summary: Israel's president has chosen the former army chief to try to build a governing coalition after an election that left both main blocs short of a majority.
body:
Israel's president, Isaac Herzog, has picked Gadi Eisenkot, the strongest challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, to make the first attempt at forming a new government after an inconclusive vote.

Herzog's office said on Saturday night that it had told Eisenkot, who leads the Yashar party, of the decision. The formal mandate is due to be handed over at a ceremony at the presidential residence in Jerusalem on Sunday. Eisenkot will then have 28 days to assemble a coalition, with the option of an extension of up to two more weeks. If he cannot do so, Netanyahu is widely expected to be given his own turn.

The election on 27 October cost Netanyahu's religious nationalist alliance its majority, yet his camp remains the biggest bloc in the 120 seat Knesset with 53 seats. Eisenkot's broad opposition grouping holds 48. Neither side can reach the 61 seats needed to govern alone.

During consultations with the president, Eisenkot won the backing of both Arab majority lists, which made record gains in the vote and could now decide the outcome. It is still uncertain whether his allies would accept their support in a coalition.

Eisenkot, 66, served as military chief of staff between 2015 and 2019. He has promised to heal divisions after years in which the country swung sharply to the right, and has pledged to confront violent settlers in the West Bank, calling recent attacks on Palestinians a form of Jewish terror tolerated by the outgoing government.

He is far from a dove, however. He rejects a Palestinian state, has vowed to end Hamas rule in Gaza and to dismantle its armed wing, and is associated with a doctrine of overwhelming force against civilian infrastructure in areas held by Hezbollah, developed during the 2006 war in Lebanon.

If he succeeds, he would end the tenure of Israel's longest serving prime minister.

title: Judge moves to appoint an investigator over Trump golf course plans
summary: A Washington court will consider naming a former federal prosecutor to test whether officials misled the bench about works at East Potomac, a public course due to close this month.
body:
A federal judge said on Saturday that she intends to appoint a former top prosecutor from Donald Trump's first term to examine whether lawyers and officials misled her about plans for a historic public golf course in Washington.

Judge Ana Reyes, who sits in the District of Columbia, wants Jessie Liu to review whether staff at the interior department and the National Park Service, and attorneys at the Justice Department, broke ethics rules or deceived the court. Liu previously served as the city's chief federal prosecutor.

The civil case began in February, when a local preservation group and two golfers sued over the administration's plan to close the East Potomac golf course and park on 15 November and rebuild it as what officials have called a world class, championship level course able to host major events. The project is one of several construction schemes the president has pursued around the capital.

Last month Reyes issued an injunction that temporarily bars the government from cutting or damaging any more trees and requires ten days' written notice before any irreversible change to the course's layout while the lawsuit continues. She now wants to know whether officials told the truth about the scale of the renovation and about the felling of hundreds of trees earlier in October.

Reyes announced a formal inquiry into the government's conduct at a hearing on 30 October. Earlier in the case she had trusted government lawyers and refused several requests from the plaintiffs to intervene. Each side has until Friday, when the next hearing is due, to comment in writing on her plan to name Liu.

As the city's then chief prosecutor, Liu handled some matters referred by the special counsel who investigated links between Trump's 2016 campaign and Russia. Trump later nominated her as associate attorney general, the third ranking post at the Justice Department, but she withdrew after opposition in the Senate over her past membership of a lawyers' group that had supported abortion rights.

A law professor at Georgetown said a judge opening such an inquiry can be a step toward holding someone in contempt of court, and reflected how hard it had been to establish who ordered the tree cutting after assurances given by government lawyers.

title: Trump tells Justice Department to look into Democrats after midterm rout
summary: The president accused newly empowered Democrats of extortion over threatened impeachments and probes, offering no evidence for his claims.
body:
President Donald Trump has instructed the Justice Department to investigate Democrats, accusing them of threatening members of his cabinet and his supporters days after the party took control of both houses of Congress.

In a social media post on Saturday, Trump called the Democrats' conduct criminal and described it as extortion of the highest order, but gave no evidence. He said some of his cabinet had been warned of impeachment and claimed, again without proof, that Democrats were targeting his donors for their political views. He singled out Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan.

Since the midterm results, Democratic lawmakers and incoming members have signalled investigations into the Trump family's business dealings, immigration enforcement, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Attorney General Todd Blanche. Once the new Congress sits in January, its committees will be able to demand documents, compel officials to testify and hold public hearings.

Representative Robert Garcia of California, expected to lead the House Oversight Committee, the chamber's main investigative panel, responded to the result with a blunt online warning to administration figures to hire lawyers.

During his second term Trump has repeatedly called for inquiries into opponents, among them former FBI director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James.

title: Pro Israel lobby money mostly backed losers in the US midterms
summary: AIPAC and allied groups still count hundreds of winners, but around two thirds of their roughly $84m went to candidates who lost.
body:
The pro Israel lobbying group AIPAC can still point to a long list of winners from Tuesday's midterm elections, but most of the money it and allied committees spent went to candidates who were defeated, according to an analysis by a foreign policy think tank.

The Quincy Institute estimates that of about $84 million spent by AIPAC, its super PAC the United Democracy Project and linked groups, around $55 million backed losing candidates. Its executive vice president argued that some candidates now see the group's money as a liability rather than an asset.

AIPAC said on the day after the vote that 234 candidates it supported, from both parties, had won. A tracking group found pro Israel committees involved in at least 32 of 35 Senate contests, spending more than $100,000 in 26 of them, with 21 of those candidates winning. AIPAC said its members would become more politically active, highlighting its backing for Democratic leaders Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries.

The costliest setback came in Michigan. About $30 million was spent on Representative Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic Senate primary, and a further $9 million reportedly backed Republican Mike Rogers, who was beaten by Abdul El Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel. In Maine, more than $4.8 million supported Senator Susan Collins, who lost to Democrat Troy Jackson. In California, over $6 million failed to stop Aisha Wahab from winning a House seat.

In Texas, James Talarico won a Senate seat by more than 12 points after openly refusing AIPAC money and voicing disgust at the war in Gaza.

The group had wins too, notably Wesley Bell in Missouri and George Latimer in New York, both helped by earlier primary spending. AIPAC said in October it would stop endorsing and giving directly to candidates after this cycle. A rival group, J Street, said it backed more than 200 candidates with over $13 million.

title: Strikes on a Sanaa village kill dozens as Yemen's front lines burn
summary: Houthi authorities blame Saudi led air raids for one of the bloodiest days of the renewed war, as government troops claim gains in Marib and al Jawf.
body:
At least 25 people, and by some Houthi counts 27, were killed on Saturday when air strikes hit al Shariya, a village in Sanaa province close to the capital, according to Houthi run media and the health ministry in Sanaa. Officials said most of the dead and roughly 30 wounded were women and children, and footage showed rescuers pulling bodies from collapsed buildings.

The Houthis blamed the Saudi led coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognised government. Neither Riyadh nor the government commented. Mahdi al Mashat, who heads the group's Supreme Political Council, promised revenge.

The raid came a day after a market in Taiz province was hit, killing about 30 people, with each side accusing the other. The Houthis say more than 50 civilians died over the two days, making it one of the deadliest stretches since fighting reignited in August.

On the ground, government forces said they had beaten back Houthi assaults in Marib with air and drone support and were pushing into Houthi held parts of al Jawf, part of an offensive launched more than a month ago. A military spokesman claimed 875 attacks on Houthi positions in a single day. None of the claims could be independently confirmed.

The Houthis, for their part, said they had fired missiles and drones at Saudi targets including King Khalid airport and oil sites around Riyadh, Khurais and Dawadmi, and a National Guard camp in Najran. The coalition said it shot down a ballistic missile over the Riyadh area.

The conflict had been largely frozen for years before the Iran war revived it. The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and over 300,000 displaced since the fighting resumed.

title: White working class voters drift towards Democrats in the midterms
summary: Voters without a college degree, long a pillar of Trump era Republican strength, moved left this year, with many pointing to prices and the Iran war.
body:
One of the most striking shifts in this year's US midterm elections came from a group that has anchored the Republican Party throughout the Trump years: white voters who did not attend university.

This bloc moved noticeably towards the Democrats, a change that helped fuel the scale of the party's gains in Congress and beyond. For years Republican strategists have treated these voters as a dependable foundation.

Voters who changed sides gave a range of reasons. High living costs featured prominently, as households struggled with prices for food, fuel and housing. Others cited the war with Iran, which has weighed on public opinion as the conflict drags on and its costs mount.

The movement matters because it chips away at the core of the coalition that twice carried Donald Trump to the White House. Even a modest loss of support among these voters can tip close contests, and Republicans are now under pressure to work out whether the swing reflects a temporary protest or a deeper break.

For Democrats, the result offers a chance to rebuild ties with working class communities they had largely lost, though holding on to them in the 2028 presidential race will be a different test.

title: Washington offers up to $20m for tips on Iran's nuclear work
summary: The State Department is seeking details on facilities, equipment and staff, while the US military sets up a new task force to choke off Iranian weapons and revenue.
body:
The United States has offered a reward of as much as $20 million for information about Iran's nuclear programme, including its facilities, its equipment and the people who work on it.

The offer comes through the State Department's Rewards for Justice scheme, which also raised the possibility of relocating anyone who comes forward. Officials said Iran's failure to meet its safeguards obligations to the International Atomic Energy Agency had left inspectors unable to keep continuous track of how many centrifuges Iran makes and holds. Centrifuges enrich uranium, which can fuel power reactors or, at very high purity, a weapon. Tehran says its programme is purely peaceful.

At the same time, US Central Command announced a new unit, Task Force Iron Gate, based in Tampa, Florida. It will work with other agencies to curb the movement of weapons and sanctioned goods across Iran's borders, and to target dual use trade and illicit income. The military says its naval blockade of Iranian ports has already stopped more than $25 billion of crude exports.

The moves follow weeks of speculation that heavier strikes could resume after the midterm elections. Before the vote, President Donald Trump said he was in no hurry, but also suggested in a television interview that the US might need to hit Pickaxe Mountain, an underground site tied to the nuclear effort, describing it as a quick job.

Both Trump and Vice President JD Vance have since linked public opposition to the war with their party's heavy losses, prompting talk that the White House may avoid escalation. On Friday Trump said Iran was desperate for a deal to end the eight month conflict.

Qatar, which is mediating, says both sides are studying its proposals. A preliminary deal in June to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz collapsed within weeks when attacks on shipping resumed.

title: Scalise and Jordan renew old rivalry in race to lead shrunken House Republicans
summary: The current majority leader and the Judiciary Committee chair are both running to become minority leader after the party lost the House.
body:
Two veteran Republicans are competing to lead their party in the House after it lost its majority in the midterm elections.

Steve Scalise of Louisiana, the current House majority leader, and Jim Jordan of Ohio, who chairs the Judiciary Committee, are both seeking the post of minority leader. The contest is a rematch between longtime rivals who have clashed for the top jobs before.

Whoever wins will take charge of a much smaller conference that must adjust to life in opposition, with Democrats set to control the chamber and the Senate from January.

The new minority leader will face the task of rebuilding after a heavy defeat, while managing relations with a White House that is now facing a hostile Congress.

title: Young voters swung hard to the Democrats and helped deliver the midterm wave
summary: Early research puts youth turnout among the highest for a midterm in three decades, with people aged 18 to 29 backing Democrats by a wide margin across racial and educational lines.
body:
Young Americans played a central part in the Democratic midterm sweep, according to early estimates from a Tufts University centre that tracks youth civic engagement.

Those figures suggest the second highest youth turnout at a midterm election in 30 years, behind only 2018, when about 31 percent of young voters cast ballots during Trump's first term.
