While voters over 45 were roughly split between the parties, people aged 18 to 29 favoured congressional Democrats by a 35 point margin across race, gender, ethnicity and education.

The swing reversed patterns seen when Trump won in 2024. Latino youth, who gave him slim majorities then, backed Democrats this year by between 10 and 15 points. Among young white men, support flipped from 63 percent for Trump two years ago to 54 percent for Democrats now. Young white women moved toward Democrats by about 15 points, and rural young voters went from an even split in 2024 to about 60 percent support for Democratic candidates. Researchers also estimate that around 15 percent of young people who voted for Trump in 2024 chose a Democratic House candidate this time.

In a group of battleground states from Florida and Georgia to Texas, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, estimated youth turnout was about 30 percent overall. Just over half of young voters ranked the economy and jobs as their top concern, followed by healthcare, the Iran war, immigration, education and the climate.

Local results underlined the shift. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic governor elect, won about 77 percent of voters aged 18 to 29. Starr County, on the Mexican border, which Trump had flipped by more than 70 points in 2024, swung back by a similar margin. In Providence, voters chose David Morales, a 28 year old democratic socialist, as the city's youngest mayor and backed a measure to pull city money from companies accused of complicity in killings of Palestinians.

Elon Musk spent close to half a billion dollars promoting Republicans, including attacks on Texas Democrat James Talarico, who still won young voters by nearly 50 points. Organisers say the next fight is inside the Democratic Party itself. By Saturday an online petition urging lawmakers to reject Hakeem Jeffries as House speaker had passed a million signatures.

title: More US officers called up as jury pool thins in USS Cole bombing trial
summary: The original panel of military officers in the death penalty case over the 2000 attack in Yemen is running out, forcing a fresh call up late next week.
body:
Jury selection in the long delayed death penalty case over the bombing of the USS Cole has run into trouble, with the pool of potential jurors shrinking faster than expected.

American military officers serve as jurors in such cases, and the original group summoned for the proceedings is being used up as candidates are questioned and excused. As a result, additional officers are being mobilised to report late next week so that a full panel can be assembled.

The case concerns the October 2000 suicide attack on the US Navy destroyer as it refuelled in the Yemeni port of Aden, an assault that killed 17 American sailors and was claimed by al Qaeda. The prosecution has spent many years winding through pretrial hearings in the military commissions system.

Choosing jurors is a delicate stage in any capital case, as each side tests whether candidates can weigh evidence fairly and consider the possibility of a death sentence. The need to bring in more officers suggests that process could take longer than planned before opening arguments can begin.

title: Schumer appears set to become Senate majority leader after Democratic sweep
summary: Despite doubts in his own caucus and anger from some activists, aides say the Democratic leader has secured enough backing to take the top Senate job.
body:
Chuck Schumer looks set to become majority leader of the US Senate after the Democrats' sweeping midterm victory, his aides say, despite lingering resistance inside his own party.

The New York senator has led Senate Democrats for years, but the election aftermath brought open questions about whether he should keep the post. Some colleagues have voiced scepticism about his leadership, and parts of the activist base have been hostile, arguing the party needs a fresh face to match the energy of its win.

Mr Schumer's team says he has now gathered enough pledges of support to be elected leader when the new Senate organises. If confirmed, he would control the chamber's agenda just as Democrats prepare to confront President Donald Trump with majorities in both houses of Congress.

The role will place him at the centre of coming fights over spending, presidential nominations and oversight of the administration. How he manages the divisions within his caucus may shape how effectively Democrats use their new power ahead of the 2028 elections.

title: Bay Area voters approve taxes to avert a transit collapse
summary: Two midterm measures won decisively, promising about a billion dollars a year for major operators that faced station closures, cancelled lines and a deepening ridership spiral.
body:
Voters across the San Francisco Bay Area strongly approved two funding measures that advocates say will pull the region's largest public transit agencies back from a fiscal cliff.

A regional sales tax of half a percent in four counties and one percent in San Francisco is projected to raise about one billion dollars a year for the four biggest operators. It won 62.2 percent support across the five counties that voted, including 78.6 percent in San Francisco. City voters also backed a parcel tax for Muni by 73.6 percent.

Without the money, Bay Area Rapid Transit faced closing as many as fifteen stations early next year, with fewer trains and higher fares. Caltrain risked shutting ten stations and ending weekend service. Muni faced cutting about a third of service, dropping twenty bus lines and suspending streetcars and cable cars. Evening service at all three was at risk.

Pandemic era ridership losses hit the Bay Area hard because agencies rely heavily on fares and because remote work remains widespread. As emergency federal aid expired, campaigners gathered hundreds of thousands of signatures to put the taxes on the ballot, including tens of thousands collected by volunteers.

Anti tax groups may still sue, which could tie funds up for years. Backers say they will defend the measures in court and want lasting state reforms before the levies expire in about fifteen years. Transit carries a large share of California ridership yet receives only a small slice of operating money from the state. Advocates hope new statewide leaders will treat Tuesday's results as proof that reliable transit remains popular.

title: Iran says it is shifting missile work into underground complexes
summary: The Revolutionary Guards claim production lines moved below ground so output can continue under bombardment, and say range limits on ballistic missiles have been lifted.
body:
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it is building underground military complexes that can keep producing and storing weapons even under heavy air attack.

At a news conference in Tehran on Saturday, Guards spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi listed what he called recent achievements, including an underground missile city that is due to be unveiled. He said missile and drone production lines had been moved rapidly from the surface into subterranean sites so that manufacturing could continue while adversaries assumed stockpiles were running down.

Mohebbi also claimed advances in stealth features that, in his account, helped Iranian missiles and drones pierce air defences in earlier fighting with the United States and Israel. He insisted every Aerospace Force weapon now in use was made with domestic knowledge rather than reverse engineered from captured gear.

The same briefing repeated a warning that previous informal limits on the range of Iranian ballistic missiles no longer apply. That follows remarks by Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei that there would be no geographical limits on Iran's reply if it were attacked again.

The conflict that began on 28 February closed the Strait of Hormuz and drove a sharp rise in energy prices. Mediation has intensified in recent days. On Friday President Donald Trump said US forces had carried out limited strikes on Qeshm Island while also claiming progress in talks with Tehran.

Iran has warned it could hit Gulf energy infrastructure if major fighting resumes. Washington has added sanctions and says a new Central Command task force will try to stop land routes used to move advanced weapons. A naval blockade aimed at Iranian oil exports remains in place.

Separately, Iranian reporting has cited earlier assessments that previous rounds of fighting damaged US bases across the region and struck Gulf infrastructure many times, with large economic losses. Those claims could not be independently verified from the public statements alone, but they form part of the narrative Tehran is pushing as it advertises hardened production sites.

title: Iraq says outsiders used its soil to attack Gulf neighbours
summary: Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein says Baghdad is investigating strikes launched from Iraqi territory against Gulf states and is talking to armed factions and Tehran about bringing weapons under state control.
body:
Iraq has evidence that external parties used its territory to launch attacks on neighbouring countries, Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said in an interview published on Saturday.

Baghdad is investigating assaults fired from Iraqi soil against Gulf states and is seeking to settle disagreements with Saudi Arabia through dialogue, Hussein said. Riyadh has accused Iran aligned groups operating in Iraq of hitting Saudi oil infrastructure. In September, Baghdad confirmed that drone attacks on the kingdom's East West pipeline originated from inside Iraq.

Hussein said the government was negotiating with Iran aligned armed factions to bring their weapons under state control, insisting the process must proceed through talks rather than force. He added that Iraq was also in contact with Tehran on the same issue.

Authorities had first set a deadline of 30 September for factions to place weapons under state authority, timed with the end of the US led coalition mandate against ISIL. Resistance pushed that deadline back to June 2027, even as Washington kept pressing for disarmament.

On the balance between Tehran and Washington, Hussein confirmed that the United States had formally asked Iraq to close all but two border crossings with Iran. He said Baghdad welcomed friendship with Tehran but rejected interference in its internal affairs.

Iraq lost about sixty billion dollars from the suspension of oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz, he said, though shipments have resumed after understandings with Washington and Tehran. After the coalition pullout, Iraq, Syria, Jordan and Turkey have formed a committee to fight remaining ISIL activity in Syria.

title: Hakeem Jeffries stands on the brink of the House speakership
summary: After the Democratic midterm sweep, the New York leader is set to become the first Black speaker, even as progressives press him over Trump, immigration enforcement and Israel.
body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York is poised to become the first Black speaker of the US House of Representatives after Democrats' decisive midterm victory.

The fifty six year old Brooklyn raised congressman would take a central role in efforts to constrain President Donald Trump in the final two years of his term. Yet some in his party doubt whether his cautious style and long record of support for Israel fit the moment.

An online petition urging lawmakers to pick someone else had gathered more than nine hundred and eighty thousand signatures by Saturday. Several newly elected progressive members have not said whether they will back him. Critics argue the speaker should answer Democratic voters rather than the party establishment alone.

Jeffries, the son of social workers from Crown Heights, worked as a corporate lawyer before winning a New York Assembly seat in 2006 and a House seat six years later. He helped broker a bipartisan criminal justice law signed by Trump in 2018, served as an impeachment manager in 2020, and in 2022 became the first Black politician to lead a party in either chamber when he succeeded Nancy Pelosi as House Democratic leader.

Where Pelosi was known for top down command, Jeffries has built a quieter consensus style. That has frustrated colleagues who want a harder line against Trump. After the election he said Americans want results rather than revenge, a line that drew sharp pushback from the left.

Progressive newcomers, sometimes called The Bloc, had floated using the speaker vote to win concessions on health care, ICE funding and weapons shipments to Israel. A comfortable Democratic majority now makes Jeffries less dependent on those votes, but also removes his old argument that Republican control blocked accountability.

His ties to pro Israel donors and past opposition to conditioning aid remain a deep divide. In July he voted against cutting annual military aid to Israel yet wrote that a meaningful change in US Israel relations was needed. No serious rival for the speakership has emerged, so the larger test will come once he holds the gavel.

title: Zaporizhzhia braces as Russian FPV drones close in on the city
summary: A region that once sheltered people fleeing occupation now faces daily drone strikes, protective street netting and talk of relocating displacement shelters.
body:
Zaporizhzhia, long a refuge for people fleeing Russian occupation further south, is itself becoming a more dangerous place as first person view drones and missiles press closer to the regional capital.

Villages south of the city have come under escalating attack. On 2 November nine Russian glide bombs hit Komyshuvakha, killing at least fifty people who had gathered for humanitarian aid at a local school. Several remain missing under the rubble.

Residents describe drones stalking streets and vehicles, a pattern already seen in Kherson, Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. One man who fled Preobrazhenka, about forty kilometres from Zaporizhzhia, said he and neighbours were in a cellar when drones struck and that he suffered burns to his arms and hands before evacuating to a city shelter. Only a handful of people remained in his village, he said.

City officials are hanging anti drone netting over streets and civilian sites, including petrol stations along the river highway. Boarded windows and wrecked buildings show how hard the threat is to blunt once drones arrive. A regional military administration official said authorities may relocate a displacement shelter to another neighbourhood if the situation worsens. Many shelter residents are elderly or lack papers needed to move on.

Earlier the same day as recent reporting from the city, Russian jet powered missiles struck a shopping mall and the main bridge into Zaporizhzhia, and an FPV drone hit a city bus. Children now walk with handheld drone detectors. Officials say they are ready to evacuate the city if required, but admit it is hard to know how many people remain because departures continue every day.

For thousands who once arrived from Mariupol and Melitopol seeking safety, the fear is that they may have to flee again.

title: US homelessness fell by a record amount in 2025, housing officials say
summary: The housing department gave President Trump the credit, while advocacy groups argued that Housing First policies of earlier administrations also drove the fall.
body:
The number of homeless people in the United States fell by a record margin in 2025, according to the Department of Housing and Urban Development.

The department presented the decline as an achievement of President Donald Trump's administration, crediting its approach to the problem for the improvement.

Groups that work with homeless people offered a different reading. They argued that the Housing First model pursued by previous administrations, which places people in stable homes before addressing other needs such as addiction or unemployment, played an important part in bringing the numbers down. The Trump administration has been critical of that model.

The figures come from an annual national estimate that has long served as the main benchmark for tracking homelessness across American cities and states.

The dispute over who deserves credit reflects a broader political argument over how best to tackle the issue, with funding decisions in Washington likely to shape whether the improvement lasts.

title: Russian strikes cut Ukrainian power ahead of Abu Dhabi talks
summary: Overnight drones and ballistic missiles hit energy sites across a dozen regions, wounding nine people, days before Ukrainian and Russian teams meet for trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi.
body:
Overnight Russian drone and ballistic missile strikes damaged Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, causing blackouts and disrupting water supplies just as temperatures fall and the first winter snow arrives.

Zelenskyy said twelve regions came under attack, with the capital Kyiv hit hardest. Officials reported nine people wounded nationwide, including one child. The wave involved more than thirty ballistic missiles and over one hundred and seventy drones.

In Kyiv, residential buildings, the North Bridge and a kindergarten were damaged. Strikes hit substations that connect the Rivne and Khmelnytsky nuclear plants to the capital and central Ukraine. Substations were also damaged in the Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv and Dnipro regions. Kyiv's mayor later said the city water system was back to normal and that about sixty percent of apartment buildings were again connected to heating. The energy minister reported power cuts in five regions.

The assault comes before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week. Zelenskyy wrote that Moscow was preparing for those talks by striking critical infrastructure.

The latest attacks follow a White House meeting on Thursday in which Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian officials and called for a more enduring ceasefire after a short truce in the southern Kherson region. Hundreds of residents of occupied Oleshky were able to leave during that six day pause.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine was counting on bipartisan American unity on security support, condemnation of Russian aggression and tougher sanctions on Vladimir Putin. He argued that consistent US backing remains vital if peace is to move closer.

title: Russian diesel tankers divert as US buyers stay away
summary: Nearly a month after Trump and Putin advertised a diesel release for American markets, no cargo has landed in the United States and several ships have changed course amid legal warnings.
body:
At least three tankers that loaded Russian diesel for the United States have altered course, casting doubt on the October arrangement President Donald Trump struck with Vladimir Putin to ease fuel prices.

Nearly a month after Trump said Russia would free more than three hundred thousand tonnes of diesel for US and global markets, with larger volumes to follow, none of that fuel has reached American ports. Retail diesel prices had nearly doubled since the start of the wider Middle East war and remain elevated.

Vessel tracking shows the Russian tanker Talisman and the Sierra Leone flagged Leruo left the Baltic port of Primorsk with US East Coast destinations, then headed toward Brazil and the Mediterranean. A third ship in the North Atlantic switched its destination to for orders. A fourth, sanctioned tanker loaded at Primorsk has been signalling an Atlantic route.

The Treasury issued a temporary sanctions exemption to allow sales, delivery and imports until 7 April, angering lawmakers who passed a fresh sanctions package in September. Congress's ban on Russian energy imports remains on the books, leaving traders exposed to civil or criminal risk and future investigations.

New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill told port and terminal operators in her state to refuse the ships and warned that profits from illegal Russian fuel trade would meet harsh penalties. She argued the White House cannot override the statutory ban. No court has yet settled the dispute.

Analysts note even the first advertised shipment would equal only about two hours of US distillate demand. Moscow insists buyers will be found and that reports of diversions are false. For now, legal fear appears to be keeping Russian diesel off the American seaboard.

title: Leaked files show a US tech firm raced to keep Israeli intel contracts
summary: Internal memos describe multi hour outages on military intelligence networks during the Gaza war, crisis repairs under wartime security, and later pitches into contested government cloud work.
body:
Leaked internal documents describe how a major US networking company scrambled to repair and expand contracts with Israeli military intelligence while the war in Gaza continued.

According to the papers, a year into the conflict Israeli military intelligence networks suffered repeated multi hour outages and crashes that undermined confidence in a key network supplier. A confidential draft memo warned that the failures, during wartime upgrades, severely affected critical operations and customer sentiment.

The company, which sells routers, servers and communications systems used by governments and militaries worldwide, has worked with Israeli security bodies for years. One 2025 document put military intelligence contracts alone at about sixty seven million dollars over three years.

When intelligence leaders threatened to cancel business, the firm activated senior staff, sent teams for months of bug fixes, and conducted on site visits under heavy security with a secretive military unit reported to be moving intelligence systems underground. After restoring service, an internal presentation billed the episode as a customer success story.

The leak also shows dozens of 2026 deals tagged for Israeli government clients, including intelligence, air force and navy accounts, many labelled as artificial intelligence work. A subsidiary analytics platform earlier this year pitched to join a contested Israeli government cloud contract already involving other large US tech firms, though it is unclear whether that deal closed.

Current and former employees organised against the military work call it a contradiction of the ethics the company markets to staff and investors. A US equal employment agency earlier found reasonable cause to believe Palestinian, Arab and Muslim staff faced a hostile workplace after October 2023; the company has disputed that finding.

Investors have called for an independent human rights review of the military business, with a shareholder vote expected this month. Watchdogs argue networking hardware sits at the base of surveillance and targeting systems even when it draws less public scrutiny than cloud or software contracts.

title: One month on, Yemen's government offensive is far from Sanaa
summary: Government forces claim fresh gains in Taiz and Lahij, but analysts see a campaign of pressure rather than victory as displacement soars.
body:
A month into the government's offensive against the Houthis, Yemen's war shows no sign of a quick end. The latest blow to civilians came on Friday, when a missile hit a market in Taiz governorate and killed dozens, with each side blaming the other.

The internationally recognised government launched the campaign against the Houthi movement, which is aligned with Iran, at the start of October. The campaign, named Dawn of Yemen, was announced on 5 October by Rashad al Alimi, who heads the Presidential Leadership Council. Its declared goals are to win back territory held by the Houthis and ultimately to retake Sanaa, the capital, which the group has controlled since September 2014.

The government relies on air cover from the Saudi led coalition alongside ground units. A central aim on the western front is to loosen the Houthi grip on the Red Sea corridor and secure the Bab al Mandeb strait, after the group seized the port of Mocha in September.

Progress has been uneven. Government forces claimed early gains near Dhubab and on mountain positions in western Taiz, and fighting later spread to Marib. Yet they also lost ground in Taiz governorate, leaving the city under a Houthi siege that is now a month old. On Friday the government said it had retaken several villages and hills in the governorate and new positions in Lahij, and claimed more than 1,200 operations against Houthi targets. Those figures could not be independently confirmed.

Analysts doubt the offensive can deliver a decisive result. One academic specialist argued that government troops are stretched across too many fronts with ageing equipment, and that the mountains ringing Sanaa make it easy to defend. In his view the campaign is better seen as a way to raise the cost of the war for the Houthis than as a bid for outright victory.

Meanwhile civilians are paying heavily. Hundreds of thousands of people have been displaced since the fighting escalated, and the Presidential Leadership Council insists its drive is irreversible, suggesting the conflict may deepen before any settlement comes into view.

title: First winter storm floods thousands of tents across Gaza
summary: Rescue crews logged about 1,500 calls for help in ten hours as rain swamped displacement camps and weakened buildings gave way.
body:
The first winter storm of the season swept across the Gaza Strip on Saturday, flooding thousands of tents and driving displaced families out into the cold and wet.

Gaza's civil defence service said it fielded roughly 1,500 calls for help within ten hours of the rain starting early in the day. In several shelter sites the water rose by around a foot, and some shelter centres were swamped entirely, leaving the people inside with nowhere to go. A spokesman warned that premature babies, the elderly and the sick face the greatest danger.

The weather also brought down structures already damaged during the war that began in October 2023. Rescuers cleared residents from a partly collapsed building in Nuseirat in central Gaza, and in the north a wall gave way under the rain, injuring two people. Images from camps in Gaza City, Khan Younis and Deir el Balah showed families wading through floodwater, bedding soaked through and children standing barefoot in mud and sewage.

In al Mawasi on the southern coast, where more than 900,000 displaced people are sheltering, rain had fallen through the night. Over 125,000 families along the shoreline are considered at particular risk of losing their tents to the sea. Local officials say more than a million displaced people now face the winter, and that the territory urgently needs about 200,000 tents together with heating supplies.

Emergency crews say they have almost nothing to hand out. The head of civil defence in Gaza governorate said his teams do not hold a single tarpaulin or tent and can only focus on saving lives.

Aid groups blame Israeli limits on shelter materials. A Palestinian NGO coordinator said only about 180 to 200 lorries enter each day, well below the 600 agreed under the ceasefire's humanitarian terms, and only around 40 of them carry aid. He said some 50,000 tents are waiting on the Egyptian side of the border and urged action before, rather than after, the next flood.

title: Sudan's war and harsh climate push child malnutrition higher
summary: Hospitals in Port Sudan are crowding three children to a bed as severe hunger among under fives climbs for another year.
body:
Children in Sudan are going hungry in growing numbers as more than three years of war, deep poverty and a harsh climate combine to strip families of food and income.

At the teaching hospital in Port Sudan, staff describe a steady stream of underweight children. One mother travelled more than two hours from her village with her five year old son, whose ribs showed clearly under his skin after repeated bouts of malnutrition. She had delayed the trip because of the distance and the fear of medical bills, and came only when she worried he might not survive. The boy spent five days on the ward.

The wider numbers are stark. The global food security monitoring system estimates that 825,000 children under five will suffer severe acute malnutrition in Sudan this year, a rise of about 7 percent on 2025. In the first half of the year, UNICEF and partner agencies treated some 174,700 children for the condition. The Port Sudan hospital alone logged 433 cases between January and August.

A nutrition counsellor there said admissions keep climbing, so the 17 bed malnutrition unit now often holds three children to a bed, raising the risk of infections spreading. Therapeutic milk and other nutritional supplies are given free with support from the World Health Organization and UNICEF, but drips and medicines remain a heavy cost for families whose incomes have collapsed.

She added that poor diets among pregnant women, worsened by displacement and hardship, are putting newborns at risk of stunted growth. Winter also tends to bring more flies, which contaminate food and water, while mosquitoes spread malaria, and malnourished children are especially vulnerable to both.

The war between the army and the Rapid Support Forces has run since April 2023, and conditions are reported to be worst in the Darfur region in the west, which had already endured two decades of conflict.

title: Eisenkot nears his chance to replace Netanyahu, but the road is steep
summary: Israel's former army chief is expected to be asked to form a government, yet assembling a stable coalition looks daunting.
body:
Gadi Eisenkot, the former head of Israel's armed forces, looks set to be given the opportunity to form a new government and take over from Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister.

That would be a remarkable turn after more than a decade in which Netanyahu has dominated Israeli politics. But turning the chance into a working government is a different matter, and the obstacles in his way are formidable.

The arithmetic from the 27 October election is part of the problem. Arab parties won a record 19 seats, enough to carry the opposition bloc past the 61 seat majority, yet relying on them is politically fraught, with Netanyahu's allies already casting doubt on the legitimacy of the Arab vote. Any coalition would also have to bridge deep differences among parties united mainly by the wish to end Netanyahu's rule.

Eisenkot's military background gives him standing with many voters, but holding together such a varied alliance, while the region remains at war, may prove the hardest mission of his career.

title: Secret Ukrainian operation clawed back ground from Russia
summary: Ukrainian commanders have opened up about a months long effort that reversed part of Russia's territorial advance.
body:
Ukraine has lifted the veil on a military operation that its commanders say helped win back some of the territory Russian forces had taken.

For months the effort was kept secret. Now commanders have allowed reporters into the bunkers and training grounds used to plan and prepare it, offering a rare look at how Ukrainian units organised a push that turned back part of Russia's gains.

The disclosure comes at a delicate time. The war is approaching its fifth year, Russian advances have slowed markedly, and the US midterm results have stirred cautious hope in Kyiv about renewed support, even as President Donald Trump talks of a deal with Moscow.

By showing that its forces can still retake ground, Kyiv appears keen to strengthen its hand both on the battlefield and in any negotiations over how the war might end. How lasting the gains prove, and whether they can be repeated elsewhere along a long front line, remains to be seen.

title: Allies read Trump's midterm defeat as a warning, not a relief
summary: Partners who spent two rocky years with Washington are not celebrating the Republican loss, seeing instead a fickle electorate and an unreliable security partner.
body:
America's closest partners are not treating President Donald Trump's midterm defeat as cause for celebration, according to reporting from allied capitals.

After two years of strained relations with the White House, officials abroad view the election result as another sign of a volatile US electorate and an unpredictable security partner rather than a simple course correction.

The caution reflects how deeply foreign policy has swung with domestic politics. Governments that rely on US guarantees on Ukraine, the Middle East and wider alliance planning now expect continued turbulence even as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress.

For capitals that hoped a rebuke at the ballot box would steady American commitments, the early signal is cooler. The midterm shock may constrain Trump at home, yet partners still see a United States whose reliability they can no longer take for granted.

title: US sanctions eight Canadian exchange firms over Iran links
summary: Treasury action targets Ontario and British Columbia money services accused of helping sanctioned Iranian networks move funds, including through crypto.
body:
The United States has sanctioned eight Canadian currency exchange businesses it accuses of helping Iranian entities dodge financial restrictions, expanding a campaign Washington brands as an effort to cut economic lifelines to Tehran and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The Treasury Department announced the measures on Friday under the label Operation Economic Outcast. It said some of the firms converted Iranian rials and other currencies into digital assets and that some activity was linked to an alleged drug trafficking figure. Firms named in public statements include Million Exchange, Amin Exchange and Cryptoyal, with operations in Ontario and British Columbia.

Sanctions freeze any United States assets the businesses hold and bar American people and companies from dealing with them, effectively cutting access to the dollar system. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Canada should not be a safe haven for facilitators who help the Iranian state and its proxies evade controls.

Canada’s financial intelligence unit said it worked with its United States counterpart to support the action and stressed routine cooperation against money laundering, terrorist financing and sanctions evasion through bilateral information sharing.

In a parallel step, the United States anti money laundering agency issued an order aimed at crypto platform MEXC Global, incorporated in Seychelles. Officials claim it handled at least sixteen billion dollars in illicit flows tied to Iran, North Korea and Russia and to other sanctioned actors, and they told American banks to block related transfers.

Earlier in the week Washington also targeted a network in India and Turkey accused of helping Iran move oil and airline related funds. US statements last week claimed pressure had pushed the rial to fresh lows and driven inflation near ninety percent.

The Canadian listings show how the Iran war’s financial front now reaches money shops and crypto rails far from the Gulf. Ottawa’s public cooperation message sits beside the practical reality that local exchange houses can still become nodes in sanctions busting chains when dollar clearing remains the choke point.

title: Record Arab vote in Israel met with a backlash of suspicion
summary: Arab parties won an unprecedented 19 Knesset seats, but Palestinian citizens of Israel say their success has been answered with fraud claims and hostility.
body:
Palestinian citizens of Israel turned out in record numbers at the 27 October election, and Arab parties came away with 19 seats in the Knesset, more than ever before. Many voters describe a rare feeling of hope, with whole families from grandparents to grandchildren going to the polls together.

Those seats matter arithmetically. They lift the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot past the 61 seats needed to form a governing coalition, making the Arab parties hard to ignore in any attempt to replace Benjamin Netanyahu.

But the reaction from parts of Israeli politics and media has been sharply hostile. Within a day of the vote, Likud and figures such as Itamar Ben Gvir accused the Arab parties of winning through bribery, intimidation, violence and forgery. The allegations have persisted even though the Central Elections Committee and the police said they found no sign of organised tampering. A hard right television channel aligned with Netanyahu repeatedly framed the high turnout in terms of terrorism, while news panels discussing Arab voters featured almost no Arab guests.

One young voter posted a video that spread widely among Palestinians, contrasting the warm language used about Arab citizens when they are seen as neighbours and symbols of coexistence with the suspicion they face the moment they seek real political influence.

In Jaffa's Ajami neighbourhood, residents see the moment against a long history. Before 1948 the city had about 100,000 Palestinian residents; afterwards fewer than 4,000 remained, confined for years under military rule. A local civic leader who grew up there described today's mix of unprecedented representation and renewed efforts to delegitimise Arab voters as part of a longer struggle simply to be accepted.

An expert on Jewish and Arab relations calls it a political crossroads for Israel, with the question of whether Arab parties can share power now central to who governs next.

title: Michigan's first Muslim senator elect sets up a Habibi PAC
summary: Abdul El Sayed has registered a leadership committee named after his trademark campaign word, days after a record breaking midterm.
body:
Abdul El Sayed, who won a Senate seat in Michigan this week and will become the first Muslim member of the US Senate, has set up a political action committee called Habibi PAC.

A filing with the Federal Election Commission dated Thursday lists it as a leadership PAC sponsored by El Sayed. Such committees sit apart from a politician's own campaign and let them raise money and donate to other candidates, their party and political groups. Lawmakers often use them to build influence with colleagues and support bids for leadership posts or committee chairs.

The name comes from the Arabic term of endearment meaning my dear, a word El Sayed used often on the trail. In his victory speech in Detroit he aimed it at Vice President JD Vance, noting with some relish that Vance will be required to swear him in come January.

He is one of several newly elected Democrats to register similar committees since Tuesday, among them the senators elect for Iowa and North Carolina and a new Arizona congressman, each with a playfully named PAC.

El Sayed, whose parents emigrated from Egypt, beat Republican Mike Rogers after a bruising race in which Donald Trump, Vance and Senator Ted Cruz questioned his loyalty and tried, without evidence, to tie him to the Muslim Brotherhood. He campaigned on spending public money on lives at home rather than on foreign governments, and on getting money out of politics, telling supporters his win showed the many can beat big money.

The irony of a money focused campaigner launching a fundraising vehicle has not gone unnoticed, but it comes amid the costliest midterms on record. Total spending is projected at about $11.9bn, up from $8.9bn in 2022, with outside spending near $3.9bn and undisclosed donations already above $1.47bn, beating the previous record set in 2024.

title: Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv area and injure two
summary: Debris damages flats and a kindergarten building as officials warn of further strikes days before planned talks in Abu Dhabi.
body:
Russian forces launched a ballistic missile attack that struck the Kyiv area on Saturday, injuring two people and damaging residential buildings as Ukraine prepares for another round of United States led talks with Moscow.

Mayor Vitali Klitschko said explosions shook the suburbs and that debris hit a five storey apartment block in a western district, with the facade of another residential building also damaged. The city’s military administration reported injuries to two civilians and damage to a building that houses a kindergarten. Officials kept warning residents that further strikes were possible hours after the first impacts.

The attack comes three days before Ukrainian and Russian teams are due to open talks in Abu Dhabi aimed at ending a war that has lasted more than four years. The last comparable round was in February. On Thursday President Donald Trump said a deal might be close after meeting Vladimir Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House, while Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian representatives linked to a localised truce she helped encourage in Oleshky. That truce expired last Sunday.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has also been pressing Western allies for concrete post war security guarantees after meetings in Brussels that covered reconstruction, next year’s funding and long term support. Officials from the United States, Britain, France, Germany and the European Union took part, alongside World Bank and private investment representatives, according to Ukrainian negotiator Rustem Umerov.

The Kyiv strike follows a deadly Russian hit on an aid distribution point in Komyshuvakha in the Zaporizhia region, where the death toll has risen to fifty according to Ukraine’s emergency service, among the deadliest civilian tolls of the year.

Military pressure around the capital therefore lands beside a crowded diplomatic calendar. Kyiv wants firm allied guarantees before any ceasefire architecture takes shape, while Moscow continues long range strikes even as envoys discuss openings in the Gulf. Residents in Kyiv are left watching both air alerts and headlines about imminent deals that have yet to stop the missiles.

title: Trump swings between threats and talk of a deal as Iran braces for more strikes
summary: After fresh US hits on Qeshm Island, Washington claims progress in talks while Iran hands out iodine tablets near nuclear sites.
body:
Since the midterm elections on Tuesday, President Donald Trump has alternated between warning Iran of devastating action and insisting a deal is close, leaving allies and adversaries alike unsure what comes next.

Having accepted a heavy Republican defeat, and conceded that the unpopular war with Iran played a part, Trump told reporters on Thursday that the US might have to destroy the rest of Iran and that people would soon find out whether he would. On Friday US forces carried out what he called minor strikes on Iranian air defences, and Iranian state media reported two missiles hitting the Suza area of Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.

Yet on the same day Trump said his administration was talking to Iranian representatives and had made a lot of progress, adding that Tehran wanted an agreement. He gave no details. On Saturday Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman rejected online claims that the talks had collapsed, saying such rumours serve only those who want the war to drag on.

Qeshm is regarded as a key Iranian naval base, and Washington says it is targeting missile launchers there to stop surface to air missiles being used against US forces. Iran's army said its air defences shot down a US drone over the island, while US Central Command described conditions as relatively calm.

Iran appears to be preparing for something larger. Health officials are reported to be distributing iodine tablets, which shield the thyroid from radiation, to communities within a few kilometres of nuclear facilities, including in the south. One official was quoted as saying Trump could no longer be trusted, and a journalist said officials had been briefed that a US strike on the deeply buried Pickaxe Mountain site was being seriously weighed.

Observers say Iran's tough conditions for reopening Hormuz to shipping, set against Trump's weakened position at home, have left the president with few easy options.

title: Herzog to name Israel coalition candidate as deadlock holds
summary: Eisenkot leads endorsements with help from Arab led parties he will not bring into government, while Netanyahu falls short after an ally withholds backing.
body:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog is due to task a candidate with forming a government on Sunday after an inconclusive election left Benjamin Netanyahu and former army chief Gadi Eisenkot both short of a clear governing majority.

During consultations that ended Thursday, sixty seven of one hundred and twenty Knesset members endorsed Eisenkot, while forty six backed Netanyahu. Eisenkot’s numerical edge depends heavily on parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, which won a record nineteen seats in October. He has ruled out bringing those parties into a coalition, leaving a political puzzle for Herzog.

Netanyahu’s endorsement count fell seven short of his bloc’s fifty three seats after United Torah Judaism, a longtime partner, withheld support over the failure to secure a military service exemption for ultra Orthodox Israelis. That fracture weakens the outgoing prime minister’s claim to first chance even as his rivals struggle to convert endorsements into a workable cabinet.

Herzog has not publicly locked in either camp, stressing both the endorsement tallies and the need for a government that can actually be formed and sustained. If no candidate succeeds within the constitutional window, Israel could face fresh elections, a path that could leave Netanyahu in a caretaker role.

Arab led parties have framed their endorsements as a bid to end Netanyahu’s tenure rather than a demand for cabinet seats they know Eisenkot will refuse. That tactical support helps Eisenkot on paper while exposing the gap between parliamentary arithmetic and coalition chemistry.

The stalemate unfolds as United States midterm results feed Israeli debates about how closely to stay tied to Trump aligned politics. Whoever Herzog picks first will still need partners across secular, religious and security minded factions that disagree on Gaza policy, conscription and the judiciary.

Sunday’s announcement will start the formal clock. It will not by itself settle whether Israel gets a new government or another stretch of caretaker rule under a prime minister who no longer commands a stable majority.

title: Houston mayor sharply limits police referrals to ICE
summary: After Democratic wins in Texas, John Whitmire orders officers to contact immigration agents only when someone faces a jailable offence.
body:
Houston’s mayor has ordered city police to curb routine cooperation with United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement, reversing a harder line he adopted earlier this year under pressure from state Republicans.

John Whitmire’s executive order says officers should contact ICE only when a person is being arrested for a jailable offence. People stopped for minor traffic violations will no longer be referred simply because an administrative immigration warrant appears in databases.

The move came days after Democrats swept statewide offices in Texas, long treated as Republican territory. Whitmire said he had consulted the newly elected governor, lieutenant governor and comptroller, framing the change as a step toward reducing fear across the city and as a possible model for other Texas municipalities. “Elections matter,” he told reporters, describing a healing process after a bitter campaign season.

Police Chief J Noe Diaz backed the order and said implementation had already begun. The policy shifts away from an April approach Whitmire adopted when then Governor Greg Abbott threatened to pull about one hundred and ten million dollars in state public safety grants. Abbott argued that a city ordinance limiting ICE contact breached a 2017 state law that bars local police from restricting cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton also sued the mayor, the city council and the police chief over that earlier ordinance. The new executive order tests how far a large Texas city can go in narrowing immigration referrals after voters handed Democrats a stronger statewide hand.

Houston is the most populous city in Texas, so the practical effect could be large for people who encounter police mainly over traffic stops. Immigrant communities have long said routine referrals turned everyday policing into a pipeline toward detention. Supporters of tighter cooperation argue that local limits complicate federal enforcement.

Whether other Texas cities follow, and whether state officials renew legal or fiscal pressure, will shape how durable Whitmire’s reset proves. For now the mayor is tying the change directly to the midterm verdict and to a bid to lower anxiety in daily encounters with police.

title: Qatar says Iran mediation remains active despite strike reports
summary: Doha dismisses claims that talks have failed and says United States officials still want a path to contain the conflict.
body:
Qatar says mediation between the United States and Iran is still underway, pushing back against reports that negotiations have collapsed even as new American strikes on Qeshm island drew fresh attention to the Strait of Hormuz.

Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed al Ansari warned that promoting claims of failure serves only those who want to prolong the war and unsettle the region. Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani told an Oxford University audience that for recent weeks Qatari mediators have worked with United States officials who show genuine intent to contain and de escalate the crisis, which he said cannot be left unresolved.

President Trump separately told reporters in Florida that American forces had carried out what he called minor strikes on Iranian air defences, describing a quick hit on an anti aircraft system. Iranian state media reported explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm and said air defences downed an American MQ 9 drone. United States Central Command described the wider situation as relatively calm while offering a large reward for information on Iran’s nuclear programme.

Trump also claimed substantial progress in talks with Tehran. Qatari officials’ public message is that diplomacy has not died with the latest kinetic incidents. That stance matches Doha’s longer role as a go between since the war began, including efforts linking nuclear inspections, Hormuz access and sanctions relief.

The contrast between strike announcements and mediation soundbites leaves regional shipping and energy markets reading mixed signals. A waterway that carries a large share of seaborne oil remains politically fragile whenever explosions are reported on nearby islands.

For now Qatar is trying to keep negotiating channels open in public as well as in private, arguing that talk of collapsed talks can become self fulfilling. Whether Washington and Tehran use that space after the midterms will determine if the next weeks bring a ceasefire framework or another cycle of limited blows and rebuttals.

title: Qatar plan ties Hormuz reopening to UN nuclear site visits
summary: Doha is pressing Tehran to let inspectors into bombed nuclear sites while Washington would ease the Hormuz blockade and free some frozen funds.
body:
Qatar is advancing a mediation package that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz in stages if Iran allows United Nations nuclear inspectors back into facilities damaged in the war with the United States.

Under the draft outline described in public briefings, Tehran would not have to ship its highly enriched uranium abroad. Options on the table include visits by International Atomic Energy Agency teams to bombed sites and measures such as down blending to lower enrichment levels, building on an earlier understanding once discussed in Cairo.

In return, the United States would lift its naval blockade on Iran in the strait and release a portion of roughly eight billion dollars in frozen Iranian assets. Iran would open a negotiated shipping lane on the second day of implementation, using a route already discussed with Oman and intended for registration with the International Maritime Organisation.

Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al Thani, the emir of Qatar, spoke with President Donald Trump about the proposal on Friday. His office stressed continued dialogue and diplomacy to prevent further regional escalation without publishing the call’s details.

Tehran has set further conditions for a lasting reopening, including an end to fighting in Lebanon, a pullback of United States forces from Iran’s coastline, steps to ease economic sanctions and talk of war reparations. Sequencing those steps remains the core dispute in the talks.

Iranian officials have sounded wary of inspectors after the midterm shock in Washington, arguing that past monitoring failed to constrain strikes on nuclear sites and could feed targeting data. Oman’s foreign minister has continued contacts on how any temporary strait arrangement would work under the law of the sea, with fees limited to services rather than tolls.

Trump is still weighing another assault on Iranian nuclear sites, though Vice President JD Vance’s comments linking the war itself to Republican midterm losses have weakened the force of those threats inside Iran. A reconstruction fund figure near three hundred billion dollars has also circulated in mediation papers without a clear funding path.

Limited exemptions already allow some Chinese, Indian, Qatari and Iraqi shipping through the waterway, according to Iranian parliamentary comments, underscoring how incomplete any blockade has been while diplomacy continues.

title: US midterm sweep hardens Israeli push to replace Netanyahu
summary: Israel’s divided opposition sees Democratic gains as a reason to unite against a prime minister tied tightly to Trump, even as longer term US support looks harder to manage.
body:
Democratic gains in the United States Congress are sharpening the case inside Israel for a coalition that can remove Benjamin Netanyahu, whose foreign policy has leaned heavily on Donald Trump and the Republican Party.

Opposition figures argue that the midterm result raises the cost of sticking with a prime minister many incoming American lawmakers treat as politically toxic. Yair Lapid urged Israelis not to write off Washington and floated a charm campaign by officials of a prospective new government to rebuild trust across the Atlantic.

That pitch drew a sharp reply from New York congressman elect Brad Lander, a Democrat who describes himself as a liberal Zionist. He said American voters, Jewish and non Jewish, want respect for international law and human rights rather than another barnstorming tour, and he pointed to the detention of Palestinian journalist Abed Abu Shehada as an example of practices that alienate allies.

Lander and two other incoming Jewish members of Congress wrote to Israel’s ambassador calling for Abu Shehada’s immediate release after reports that masked security officers took him from his home without a warrant and questioned him about a podcast interview.

For decades bipartisan backing in Washington was treated as a strategic foundation for Israeli security policy. Critics say Netanyahu broke that pattern by aligning so closely with one American party. They now warn that the gamble looks dangerous after Republicans lost ground.

At the same time, many in Israel read the midterms as part of a longer shift that will constrain any future prime minister, not only Netanyahu. Military and diplomatic support from the United States remains central, so whoever forms the next government will still have to navigate a cooler and more conditional mood in Congress.

The opposition remains split on personalities and red lines, including how to handle parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel. The midterm shock does not invent a majority, but it raises the political price of failure to assemble one while Netanyahu stays closely identified with Trump’s camp.

title: Zelenskyy set for UK state visit in 2027
summary: Britain plans a grand ceremonial welcome marking five years since Russia’s full scale invasion of Ukraine.
body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is to receive a United Kingdom state visit in 2027, a ceremonial honour planned to mark five years since Russia’s full scale invasion.

State visits are among the highest formal welcomes Britain extends to foreign leaders, typically pairing palace pageantry with substantive talks. Scheduling the occasion for the fifth anniversary year underscores how central Ukraine remains to British foreign and defence policy even as United States politics shift after the midterms.

The announcement lands while Russian strikes continue against Ukrainian cities and as Washington hosts Russian envoys for talks that have excluded Kyiv from some sessions. British officials have repeatedly argued that military aid, training and long term security commitments must continue regardless of fluctuations in American congressional maths.

A 2027 date gives planners time to arrange the full ceremonial programme and related bilateral meetings. It also offers Kyiv a high visibility platform in London at a moment when European allies are debating post war guarantees, reconstruction finance and how to deter another Russian offensive.

For Zelenskyy the visit would showcase enduring G7 support after years of wartime diplomacy. For Britain it signals that Ukraine policy remains a multi year national commitment rather than a short emergency response. The war’s fifth anniversary framing ties the pomp to a solemn milestone rather than a victory parade, reflecting a conflict that still lacks a settled endgame.

title: Trump midterm defeat fuels talk of a US retreat
summary: Analysts say American retrenchment after the vote could reorder Middle East power balances and open space for China.
body:
Donald Trump’s heavy midterm defeat has intensified debate over whether the United States will pull back from overseas commitments, with particular attention on the Middle East balance of power and on opportunities for China.

American retrenchment talk is not new, but the scale of Republican losses gives allies and rivals fresh reason to test Washington’s appetite for sustained military, financial and diplomatic engagement. In the Gulf and Levant, governments that hedged between American security guarantees and other partners may adjust faster if they judge Congress less willing to fund open ended campaigns.

The Iran war already strained United States political support at home. Voters punished costs that showed up in energy prices and in fears of wider escalation. A Congress now dominated by Democrats can constrain presidential war powers and spending even while Trump still controls day to day executive tools until the next presidential contest.

China watches those gaps. A perception that Washington is tired of Middle East crises can encourage deeper Chinese commercial and diplomatic inroads, from energy ties to mediation offers, without Beijing needing to match American military footprints.

None of that locks in a clean withdrawal. The United States still runs major forces, sanctions machinery and alliance networks across the region. What changes after a midterm shock is the credibility of threats and promises that rely on future money and authorisations from a hostile legislature.

For regional capitals the practical question is sequencing: whether to wait out Trump’s remaining term, court Democratic leaders early, or diversify security partnerships now. The retreat narrative will shape those choices even if actual force levels move more slowly than the headlines.

title: Justice Department drops its bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots
summary: The Trump administration has abandoned a lawsuit over thousands of mail in votes after the Supreme Court refused to back it before polling day.
body:
The US Justice Department has dismissed its lawsuit against California over roughly 20,000 mail in ballots, ending a high profile legal fight over the state's midterm vote count.

The Trump administration had sought to have the ballots set aside, but the effort suffered a decisive setback before election day when the Supreme Court rejected it. With that ruling in place and the votes already cast and counted, the department has now withdrawn the case.

The suit was part of a wider push by the administration to challenge voting procedures in states run by Democrats, particularly around postal voting, which President Donald Trump has repeatedly attacked as open to fraud without producing evidence of widespread abuse.

The dismissal comes as the administration weighs its response to a midterm result that handed Democrats control of Congress.

title: US voters reject data centre projects in almost every midterm ballot fight
summary: Across 41 local measures, communities moved to block or limit large computing sites, with only one small North Dakota town defeating tighter review rules.
body:
American voters used Tuesday's midterm ballots to push back against data centre building, rejecting or limiting projects in nearly every local contest that put the issue to a vote.

An election monitoring project tracked 41 ballot measures tied to data centres across the country. Voters were on course to reject data centre development in all but one of those fights, with two races still being counted but expected to favour limits. The sole clear exception was Harwood, North Dakota, a town of fewer than 800 people, where voters defeated a measure that would have required independent reviews of large industrial projects such as data centres before construction.

The results follow months of local anger over power use, water demand, noise and land consumption linked to the computing halls that train and run artificial intelligence systems. A September poll had found that about 70 percent of respondents opposed new data centres near their communities. Democrats sought to channel that backlash during the campaign, and Tuesday's local tallies suggest the opposition translated into votes even where national party contests dominated headlines.

For the technology industry the message is practical. Expansion plans that assume easy local approval now face a map of hostile ballot outcomes, slower permitting and higher political risk just as investors debate how midterm Democratic gains will shape federal rules on artificial intelligence infrastructure. For residents the votes were often framed more simply as a stand over electricity bills, water and who decides what gets built next door.

title: Beijing confirms talks on a historic Xi Trump Putin meeting
summary: China says a three way summit is under discussion while Ukraine faces fresh strikes on Kyiv and presses allies for Patriot missiles and postwar security guarantees.
body:
China has confirmed that it is discussing a historic meeting between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, a format that would place the Ukraine war and great power bargaining on the same stage.

Foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said this week that such a gathering was under discussion. Analysts watching the track say Moscow would likely use any three leader summit to pull Beijing and Washington closer to Russian positions on Ukraine. Advisers around Trump have separately cautioned him against letting Ukraine dominate those talks, according to public briefings circulating after the Chinese remarks.

On the ground the war did not pause for summit talk. Ukraine again came under Russian attack on Saturday. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy repeated calls for allies to supply missiles for US made Patriot batteries to defend Ukrainian cities. Kyiv's mayor reported that an early Saturday missile strike damaged a residential building in the capital, part of weeks of near constant pressure on urban areas and energy sites.

Zelenskyy has also pressed Western partners for specific guarantees on how postwar security support would work once fighting with Russia ends. His comments followed two days of allied discussions in Brussels that brought together officials from the United States, Britain, France, Germany and the European Union, along with the World Bank and a major US investment group, according to Ukraine's lead negotiator.

The diplomatic calendar now holds two competing stories at once: a possible Xi Trump Putin encounter that could redefine leverage over any settlement, and a Ukrainian push for air defence munitions and written security promises before winter deepens the cost of damaged power and housing.

title: Trump says US carried out minor strikes on Iranian air defences
summary: The president described a short attack on an antiaircraft system after Iranian media reported explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
body:
President Donald Trump has said United States forces carried out what he called minor strikes on Iranian air defences on Friday, hours after Iranian state media reported explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.

Speaking to reporters in West Palm Beach, Florida, Trump said Iranian forces had built a limited antiaircraft device and that American units knocked it out in about 15 minutes, perhaps five. He framed the action as part of a pattern of small strikes rather than a new major campaign.

Iranian state media said the sound of two explosions was heard in the Suza area of Qeshm, a large island that sits on the oil shipping choke point disrupted since the US Iran war began earlier this year. Iran's state broadcaster also aired an army claim that Iranian air defences had intercepted and destroyed an American MQ9 drone over the island. US Central Command, asked about reports of explosions, described the wider situation as relatively calm and declined further public comment.

Friday's action is the first publicly claimed American strike since Republicans suffered a heavy midterm defeat that Trump and other Republicans have linked in part to the Iran war and higher fuel prices. It also follows limited American strikes earlier in the week around Qeshm, Hengam and the nearby mainland near Bandar Abbas that Washington had called defensive.

Diplomatic tracks remain active even as the military signalling continues. Trump said there had been a lot of progress in talks with Tehran, without releasing details of any draft terms. The mix of another limited strike near Hormuz and renewed talk of negotiation keeps markets and regional governments watching whether the week ends in escalation or in a narrower bargaining window.

title: US measles cases top 5,000, highest tally in 35 years
summary: Health officials report 5,182 confirmed infections, mostly in outbreaks, as kindergarten vaccination coverage slips and children and teenagers account for most cases.
body:
United States health officials have recorded 5,182 confirmed measles cases, the highest national total since 1991, in a surge that is hitting children and teenagers hardest.

Figures released by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention show children under five making up 18 percent of cases and those aged five to 19 accounting for 41 percent. Together, children and teenagers represent about 59 percent of confirmed infections. The vast majority, 4,993 cases, were linked to outbreaks rather than isolated introductions.

The climb comes as measles vaccination coverage among kindergarten pupils has fallen from 95.2 percent in the 2019 to 2020 school year to 92.4 percent in 2025 to 2026. Confirmed cases so far in 2026 are more than double the 2,289 recorded across the whole of 2025.

Measles is highly contagious and preventable with routine immunisation. Public health agencies have warned for several years that slipping school entry coverage would reopen gaps large enough for outbreaks to take hold. The latest national count turns that warning into a measured reverse of decades of progress, with families, schools and clinics now managing a disease many American parents had rarely seen.

title: Qatar urges US and Iran not to wait for a perfect peace moment
summary: Doha's prime minister says both sides must reach a deal to end the war now, as Iranian state media report missiles striking Qeshm Island without casualties.
body:
Qatar's prime minister has urged the United States and Iran to strike a peace deal without waiting for ideal conditions, as fighting continues and fresh reports emerge of missiles hitting an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz.

Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, who also serves as foreign minister, said during an interview at Oxford University that Washington and Tehran cannot afford to wait for a "perfect moment" to end the war. His appeal frames mediation from Doha as a live option at a time when American politics is still absorbing a midterm defeat widely linked to the conflict, and when Iranian leaders are weighing nuclear and security proposals already circulating in public summaries.

Iran's official news agency IRNA said two missiles struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. Semi official Iranian outlets reported that there were no casualties. The island has featured in earlier American and Iranian claims about limited defensive or retaliatory action, and any confirmed strike near the shipping choke point raises immediate questions for oil transit and regional insurance markets.

The twin messages, a Qatari push for talks and another incident around Hormuz, underline how diplomacy and military signalling are moving in parallel. Public facts do not yet show whether the Oxford remarks were coordinated with Tehran or Washington, or whether the Qeshm reports will harden either side's terms. They do show Doha pressing both capitals to treat a ceasefire window as urgent rather than hypothetical.

title: Midterm sweep deals a blow to Trump's Iran war narrative
summary: America's costliest election still produced a Democratic victory widely read as a rebuke of the conflict, leaving Republicans struggling to regain control of the story.
body:
Republicans poured money into the most expensive midterm contest in American history, yet voters delivered a Democratic sweep that many analysts now cast as a direct rebuke of President Donald Trump's Iran war narrative.

Public tallies put total midterm spending near $12bn, much of it on advertising, with a majority of that money backing Republican candidates. The result was a Democratic victory on a scale not seen in half a century. In the aftermath Trump, long accustomed to turning crisis into political theatre, appeared to lose grip on the story that had framed the campaign.

Coverage of the defeat has linked the repudiation not only to domestic discontent but also to the US Israeli war on Iran. That reading sits beside Trump's own remarks blaming the conflict and higher fuel prices for Republican losses, and beside comments from Vice President JD Vance listing the Israel relationship among reasons voters walked away.

The political meaning is still contested inside the Republican Party, where strategists debate whether to defend the war as unfinished business or to distance the 2028 field from it. What the public record already shows is narrower and harder to spin: a historic spending spree failed to sell the administration's account of the conflict, and Congress now returns with Democrats holding new leverage over war funding, oversight and any settlement track.

title: Hundreds of Palestinian couples marry in a Gaza mass wedding
summary: About 250 couples took part in a shared ceremony organised through a UAE backed humanitarian relief campaign as the war grinds on across the enclave.
body:
About 250 Palestinian couples have married in a mass wedding in Gaza, a public celebration of new family life staged while the war continues to reshape daily existence across the enclave.

Organisers said the event was arranged by Operation Chivalrous Knight, a humanitarian relief campaign backed by the UAE. Couples gathered to exchange vows and mark beginnings that many families have deferred under bombardment, displacement and the collapse of ordinary civilian routines.

Mass weddings have periodically appeared in Gaza during earlier rounds of conflict as a way to cut costs, share scarce resources and assert normal life under abnormal pressure. This gathering stands out for its scale and for the Gulf funding channel named by organisers, at a moment when reconstruction, shelter and basic services remain far short of need.

Public reports do not list individual names, dowry arrangements or whether participants were newly displaced. They do confirm a large, organised ceremony framed as both relief and defiance: a claim that courtship, marriage and family continuity continue even when housing, work and safety do not.

title: US held secret talks with Iran on deporting Iranians amid the war
summary: Court filings show the Trump administration discussed removals through a third country even while calling Tehran an enemy, and a judge ordered advance notice before any deportation.
body:
The Trump administration held secret talks with Iran about deporting Iranians even as the war between the two countries continued, according to court documents unsealed in a US immigration case.

Filings show that as recently as mid October the administration said it had plans to remove Iranians through an unnamed third country, though it was unclear when any such transfers would begin. The case arises from a lawsuit that alleges violations of national immigration rules.

A federal judge ordered the government to give the court 24 hours' notice of any finalised plan to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country, and five days' written notice before carrying out such a removal. During a hearing the judge pressed justice department lawyers on the logic of sending people back to a country the president has described as lawless and as an enemy of the United States, warning of a serious threat of death. The government attorney replied that the United States was executing lawful removal orders.

The disclosure lands while combat and diplomacy with Tehran both remain active, and while Stephen Miller, a chief architect of hardline deportation policy, has just been named White House chief of staff. Public records do not show how many people were targeted, which third country was discussed, or whether Iran agreed to accept returnees. They do show a wartime administration pursuing immigration enforcement against nationals of a state it is fighting, under court supervision that now requires advance notice before any flight.

title: Israel closes Hebron's Ibrahimi Mosque to Palestinians for Jewish holiday
summary: Palestinian worshippers and staff are barred while thousands of Israeli visitors are expected at the contested West Bank holy site through Saturday evening.
body:
Israeli forces have closed the Ibrahimi Mosque in occupied Hebron to Palestinian worshippers as thousands of Israeli settlers gather for a Jewish religious observance.

The Palestinian Ministry of Religious Endowments said worshippers and mosque employees were barred from entering and that the call to prayer had been suspended. The mosque director said Israeli authorities planned to open the prayer halls and courtyards exclusively to Israelis. The closure began on Friday afternoon and is set to last until 10pm on Saturday.

The timing matches an annual Jewish observance linked to Sarah, traditionally believed to be buried at the site with the Prophet Abraham and other family members. Jews know the compound as the Cave of the Patriarchs. Israeli forces said they expected about 20,000 visitors and deployed hundreds of security personnel. Troops tightened checkpoints across Hebron's Old City and restricted some residents from entering or leaving their homes.

Under a 1997 Hebron agreement, Israel held security control of the Old City while the Palestinian municipality kept planning powers. In June, Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich announced a takeover of those planning powers, raising fears of a push toward exclusive Jewish use of the site.

The closure comes days after Israeli forces ended a 10 day siege of Hebron that brought hundreds of arrests, 15 home demolitions and the displacement of more than 3,300 Palestinians. Settlers have steadily expanded their presence in the Old City, seizing properties and planting new outposts under military protection. The dual holy site remains one of the most sensitive flashpoints in the West Bank.

title: Trump names Stephen Miller White House chief of staff after midterm losses
summary: The hardline immigration adviser will replace Susie Wiles on Monday as Democrats prepare to take both chambers of Congress.
body:
President Donald Trump has named Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff, moving Susie Wiles to his political operation three days after Republicans lost control of Congress.

Trump said on Friday that Miller, one of his closest advisers across both presidential terms, would start on Monday. He thanked Wiles for her service and said she would shift to the Trump Political Operation. Speaking to reporters, he said Wiles had done a very good job but that moves sometimes had to be made.

Miller has been the main architect of the administration's hardline border and deportation policies, a flashpoint in the midterm campaign. He joined Trump's first election team as an adviser in 2016 and stuck with him after the 2020 defeat. Trump called him one of his most trusted advisers and said he understood politics well.

Wiles submitted her resignation on Thursday night after Republicans lost the House and Senate, according to US officials. Three sources said she quit because of the election losses. She described serving as chief of staff as the honour of a lifetime and said her commitment to Trump and the mission would not change even as her role did. Last month Trump had insisted there was zero chance she would be replaced soon.

Democrats are expected to open investigations into Miller once they take control of both chambers in January. House Democrat Robert Garcia, lined up to lead the Oversight Committee, said he would keep probing what he called misconduct linked to immigration raids. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries denounced the appointment in sharp terms.

The shake up comes as other senior figures leave. Justice Department officials including the head of the national security division and a Florida US attorney have resigned in the wake of the midterm rebuke. Trump was widely expected to reshuffle staff after Democrats netted Senate seats and a clear House majority, with some races still being counted.

title: Senior US Justice Department officials resign after Democratic midterm sweep
summary: A Florida US attorney known for Trump backed probes and the head of the national security division quit as the administration braces for congressional investigations.
body:
Two more senior figures have left the United States Justice Department in the wake of the Democratic midterm victory, extending an exodus of Trump aligned officials.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said Jason Reding Quinones, the US attorney for the Southern District of Florida, submitted his resignation on Friday. Quinones had overseen and expanded a federal probe into Russia's alleged role around the 2016 election, a case Trump has long cast as a political witch hunt even after a special investigator found no direct collusion with his campaign. Critics say the department pursued politically charged investigations at the president's urging.
